search_index.description: The new generation of November novel writing Plus: What to do after you actually finish writing your book. (Issue #453) For 25 years, writers knew that November meant writing a novel. Or at least …
search_index.content: Medium The new generation of November novel writing | by The Medium Newsletter | The Medium Blog | Nov, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in The Medium Blog · The official source of news and updates about Medium Writing NaNoWriMo Novel November Novel Writing The new generation of November novel writing Plus: What to do after you actually finish writing your book. (Issue #453) The Medium Newsletter Sent as a Newsletter · 5 min read · Nov 4, 2026 -- 16 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Students writing notes, via Onwuka Glory / Wikimedia Commons . For 25 years, writers knew that November meant writing a novel. Or at least 50,000 words of one. National Novel Writing Month, or NaNoWriMo, was an internet challenge where writers would attempt to write a 50,000-word novel (or 50,000 words of a novel, even if it wasn’t complete) over the 30 days of November. But in 2025, the nonprofit who organized the annual event announced that they were dissolving . Despite the end of an organized event, many writers have continued the tradition as an informal November novel-writing challenge . In this issue, we’re seeing what writers on Medium are doing, and what advice they can give for those who want to challenge themselves, too. NaNoWriMo got me through more Seasonal Affective Disorder blips than therapy ever did. — Lacey in Self Publishing Adventures , I Still Need NaNoWriMo — Even If It No Longer Exists Finding your challenge “The idea of writing a novel (approximately 50,000 words or 1,667 words per day) during the month of November isn’t going anywhere ,” writes Daley W. in Worldbuilding Wednesday . “In fact, new communities and platforms have taken up the cause in the wake of the NaNoWriMo shutdown.” While the end of NaNoWriMo meant the end of the formal, singular challenge, the writing community around it has since banded together. A number of organizations and communities have started their own versions of it, and for 2026 Daley shares three potential options : Novel November by editing tool ProWritingAid, which follows the same basic challenge as NaNoWriMo (50,000 words over the course of the month); Worldember by tabletop game and world-building site World Anvil, which challenges would-be builders to create 10,000 words of worldbuilding writing on their platform; The November Novel Challenge from WritingHabit allows users to make their own custom word count for the month to avoid the massive 50,000-word goal. In the publication Friends of National Novel Writing Month , former Medium employee Julie Russell writes about a new challenge organized by Chris Baty , the original founder of NaNoWriMo: NaNo 2.0 . Like other challenges, NaNo 2.0 is much more flexible than the original, allowing writers to right-size their novel-writing month; Russell, for example, writes, “This November, I want to get to know this one character. Precisely how I‘ll get to know her will be the mystery.” The organization features a new-for-2026 customizable word count tracker. Although the NaNoWriMo site is now offline, there are still lots of resources for writers unsure of what to do. The original resources can be found on the Internet Archive ; more formal events like ProWritingAid’s Novel November offer workshops. And Medium writers who have taken this journey have plenty of advice for you, like lessons for getting through the middle of a novel from Felicia C. Sullivan or making sure you don’t artificially limit yourself by dismissing certain genres from Joshua Grasso . (Check out the Novel Writing topic page for more advice). But the most important thing to keep in mind, as Shelby Sullivan writes, is: “If you make it to the end, you win.” We can be so thrilled with our own created world, our characters or our prose that we presume the reader will be equally engrossed. There is no sure test for the quality of our hook. Perhaps the best test comes by employing a range of honest readers who are prepared to risk wounding us by saying whether or not they would bother reading on. — James Parsons in Never Stop Writing , Your Opening Chapter Isn’t Just About a Hook What happens next The point of challenges like NaNoWriMo and Novel November are to simply get you in the habit of writing. But actually getting the words down is only the first step. “Yep, after finally writing it, you still have a lot more work to do,” writes David Graham in Story Maniacs . He recently published his first novel, but it was “ a very difficult and up-and-down journey ” to get there. The first and maybe most important lesson he has for aspiring novelists: “I had learned how to write a novel, which was why my stories were always being praised, but I hadn’t learned how to edit one.” Graham took courses, hired professional copyeditors, and worked with beta readers who did not know him to get his novel to the point where it could be published. “Overcoming writer’s block is hard at any time,” writes Jemma Pollari in the Writing Cooperative , “but especially when you’re trying to make the manuscript ‘better .’” She suggests asking yourself some hard questions when you’re stuck, like “Is the scene boring, even to you?” “Here’s what no one told me,” Attila Vágó writes in a retrospective on his first novel. “From writing the first words to going live on Amazon in paperback format, it took over four years. Not the writing. That took the least amount of time. Everything else took a lot longer.” So as you finish up your challenge, bask in the achievement — but if you’re aiming to actually publish your novel, know that there’s still lots of work to do. Thankfully, you’re not alone, and can learn from other novel writers on next steps. Good luck! A final thought If you can’t let go of your feeds, don’t just call it “doomscrolling;” instead, think of it as “ information anxiety .” Psychiatrist Jud Brewer MD PhD recently wrote about “that restless, compulsive need to know everything that’s hap

It makes your life better. | by The Medium Newsletter | The Medium Blog | Nov, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in The Medium Blog · The official source of news and updates about Medium Writing Tk Medium Writing Tips Write by any means necessary. It makes your life better. Publish or perish? Our new app, TK, helps you write and thrive. (Issue #454) The Medium Newsletter Sent as a Newsletter · 5 min read · 5 days ago -- 14 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Frieze ornament, via Metropolitan Museum of Art / Wikimedia Commons In the AI era, “it’s easy to just say that writing is more valuable,” writes Medium CEO Tony Stubblebine in “ We are betting on human intelligence ”. “But as people who love writing, we see the value of writing as permission to do something we already wanted to do, which is write more.” Earlier this week, Medium publicly launched TK , a private, agentic notebook app to help you craft writing that compounds into deep thinking. It’s a home for all your writing: ideas, notes, journals, research, drafts. If Medium is built around a polished, published post, TK is for the drafts folder, group chats, outlines, NaNoWriMo attempts , wikis, and save files with suffixes like “Final_REALFINAL_v1-B17.” TK is built around what Stubblebine calls in an interview with The Verge “private blogging.” The focus isn’t publishing; it’s meant to just get you writing. In this issue — and we know we’re preaching to the choir here — we wanted to make a case for why just writing is more important. I once heard that great writing is like having a conversation at the pub after a few glasses of wine, chatting with friends. — Romy Elsewhere , Why Writing Matters To Me The pain — and power — of writing “Let’s be honest,” writes Lysa Cohen . “Writing is one of those things people keep telling you is important, like flossing or eating vegetables. But most of the time, it feels like a lot of effort for not much payoff .” This contradiction tortures so many of us: We may love writing, but the act of actually writing can be a nightmare. Matt Lillywhite will often “type a sentence, stare at it for a few seconds, decide it was terrible, and delete the whole thing .” Amy Shearn writes that “this whole process reminds me a bit of giving birth .” But the point is to not let the friction of writing get in the way. “These days, when I have writer’s block, I don’t try to figure out how to write the whole article,” Lillywhite writes. “I just tell myself I need to write one sentence.” “The task, for those of us who want to keep writing, is to process the frustration,” argues Shearn. “You’re still here, aren’t you?” When Cohen’s students are hostile to writing, she tells them “writing gives you power,” she writes. “The power to explain, persuade, entertain, and even roast your friends in a way that’s clever enough to make them laugh instead of get mad.” The secret is to find the way to get past that pain and just start writing. When you get in a narrative flow, and the words meld together seamlessly, there are few things in life that can compare. — Joshua Brandt in Crow’s Feet: Live As We Age , I Had Writer’s Block for Twenty Years How TK can help Press enter or click to view image in full size TK, via tk.xyz TK is designed to get you past the pain and write more. Tony Stubblebine writes that TK tackles three goals : “Easy to write.” The app is full of tools to make writing easier. There are simple, easy-to-use prompts that can serve as inspiration. It also turns the classic writing placeholder TK (meaning To Come ) into a callable prompt for an unintrusive AI writing assistant. For example, a writer can type ‘@TK share the paragraph I wrote the other day’ or ‘@TK when does Daylight Savings Time end?’ and it will fill it in while you write, so you don’t get sidetracked. “Easy to think.” TK is structured around communal writing and making it as easy to receive feedback as possible, from both human writers and AI. Writing can be shared with beta readers and editors with a link, similar to other online writing tools like Google Docs; AI feedback can give you instant notes before you go public. “Easy to feel like your writing matters.” TK is made for you to “embrace the mess,” Stubblebine writes. Instead of having to adapt how you write to a new organization system, TK pulls everything together for you: It pulls worldbuilding docs, drafts, or other writing, and helps you find connections in your own writing to make something even better. The writers who tested out TK have found these tools helpful in getting them to write more. “What has been most useful to me is having a warehouse for my thoughts and ideas ,” writes Annette Couchenour , “including unfinished pieces I’m still thinking through, and seeing how TK can connect the dots across my writing.” When Kaili Bisson used TK’s daily notes and nudges , she “discovered that ordinary thoughts often become meaningful when you give them somewhere to land.” “The one good thing I found during all of this was a new community of writers ,” writes Alex Rowe . TK “has a neat library system where you can connect with other users and talk about topics or share your work.” For Medium VP of Content Scott Lamb , TK removed a great deal of the friction that made a daily writing habit a chore. “Over the last few months, my writing’s picked up, almost without me noticing,” he writes. “I’ve only missed four days of writing in the last month.” We encourage you to try TK . It’s free for anyone with a Medium account. Find a community. Answer a prompt. Get some feedback and find some insight. See if it can help you write every day. The more you write, the better your life gets. A final thought On this topic, we want to leave you with Sethu Raman Omanakuttan . He’s an app builder, but has found there’s a certain symmetry between building a tech product and writing a poem . No matt

search_index.content: Medium That Day I Went Crazy and Ended My Marriage | by Kerala Goodkin | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Member-only story Relationships Marriage Family Divorce Feminism That Day I Went Crazy and Ended My Marriage The all-too-familiar story that denies women their fury and pain Kerala Goodkin 11 min read · Nov 12, 2024 -- 77 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Watch out, world… crazy woman on the loose! Photo by sdominick/Getty Images Signature According to the man I married, I went crazy and that’s why our marriage is ending. I went crazy on April 20, 2024, the night I couldn’t sleep. By the way, I recommend going crazy in April. By then, the days are getting longer, the weather is finally improving, and you can go on long walks, perhaps occasionally muttering to yourself for the full effect. It wasn’t on my to-do list to go crazy on that particular night in April. I couldn’t sleep because I was furious, and I wanted a hit of cannabis to calm my nerves. The cannabis was upstairs, where my husband was either listening to music or sleeping on the couch. He often fell asleep on the couch. Usually the music was still blaring from his headphones when he faded into unconsciousness. If I awoke after midnight and felt the coolness of the sheets beside me, I used to go fetch him. It was the wifely thing to do. I didn’t want him to get a crick in his neck and I wanted his body next to mine, even though that same body often awoke me multiple times a night with its snoring — simultaneously erratic and incessant. Erratic and incessant — like his fury. Written by Kerala Goodkin ⁠ 24K followers · 933 following Award-winning writer. Interrupting notions of what it means to be a mother, woman, worker, and wife. Although rice has become the… | by Layla Rharabi | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in The history of Rice in China. Layla Rharabi 5 min read · Sep 9, 2021 -- 3 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Riz blanc ( https://images.app.goo.gl/5sXGTqcWXqjevbMa9 ) Although rice has become the indispensable staple of modern Asia,historical Chinese civilization emerged in the arid north, a region unfit forrice cultivation. People settled into agricultural villages in the YellowRiver valley as early as 7000 BCE, growing the nutritious grain millet. Rice domestication probably took place in a number of hearths, stretching from South-east Asia to the Yangtze River valley, which eventually became the Chinese agricultural heartland. The seemingly more primitive nomadic lifestyle actually developed later, about 2000 BCE, when Turkic peoples brought horseback riding skills to the western steppe. Chinese cuisine thus developed from earliest times with the recognition of regional differences. The Chinese state acknowledged thisagrarian basis, and the ancient classics ranked food as the first of eightconcerns of the government. According to legend, the founder of the Shang dynasty (c. 1766–1122 BCE) appointed his cook Yi Yin to be prime minister, and the cooking cauldron served as the prime symbol of government. Emperors conducted elaborate ritual sacrifices to propitiate the gods and ancestors, thereby ensuring good harvests. After deposing the Shang, the Western Zhou dynasty (c. 1040–771 BCE) asserted it’slegitimacy to rule, the Mandate of Heaven, by claiming descent from the millet god. The regulation of food remained a central concern with the rise of Chinese social philosophy during the Eastern Zhou dynasty (770–256 BCE). Confucius (551–479 BCE), who emphasized gentlemanly conduct and strict observance of social hierarchies, extended this decorum to the finest details of food preparation. The Analects described his fastidious behavior when dining: “Undercooked foods he does not eat, and foods served at improper times he does not eat. Meat that is improperly carved, he does not eat, and if he does not obtain the proper sauce, he will not eat.” Conflating personal behavior with the body politic, Confucius likened a well-planned meal to a well-governed state. Mencius (372–289 BCE) similarly averred that the primary duty of a ruler was to ensure that his subjects were properly fed. Even the draconian Legalist school, which opposed Confucian thought on most subjects, agreed that productive agriculture was essential for the well-being of the state. The first world cuisine 9A concern with balance and form had already infused Chinese cooking methods and eating rituals by the Eastern Zhou. The first step in preparing a propermeal lay in balancing staple grains with condiments such as meat and vegetables. Of necessity, the poor ate large bowls of rice or millet porridge, supplemented by soybeans, but the food canons (dietary guides) advised the wealthy likewise to avoid excessive quantities of rich foods. Confucius again set the example: “Though there is plenty of meat, he will not allow it to overcome the vitalizing power of the rice. ” Patterns of combining flavors and chopping ingredients, which are still distinctive characteristics of modern Chinese cuisine, had also been established; indeed, the cook’s art of balancing the five flavors (salty, bitter, sweet, sour, and piquant) came to mirror the cosmological balance of five elements (earth, wood, fire, water, and metal). Cuisine likewise contributed to the formation of social hierarchies. The Rites of Zhouassigned more than 2,200 attendants, over half of an idealized imperial household, to the preparation of food and drink. Other works set the proper number of meat and vegetable dishes according to rank (a high minister earned eight while a lower official got only six) and age (with more variety reserved for the elderly).All people were assumed to eat four bowls of grain daily. The classics also prescribed strict rules foretiquette, giving particular attention to the deference owed by people of lower rank to their superiors. Prepared for an elite audience, these textsdenounced the boorish behavior of the lower classes, althoughcommoners doubtless maintained their own standards for proper conduct. The Chinese predilection for opulent banquets coexisted uneasily with philosophical teachings of simplicity and spiritual nourishment. The Daodejing, attributed to the sixth-century mystic Laozi, warned simply: “The five flavors confuse one’s palate.” Mozi (470–391 BCE) explicitly denounced elite gourmandizing: “There is no need of combining the five tastes extremely well or harmonizing the different sweet odours. And efforts should not be made to procure rare delicacies from far away countries. ” A system of humoral medicine ultimately arose from this tension between luxury and simplicity. Applying the Daoist concept of yin and yang to foods, Chinese physicians advised patients to maintain good health by balancing “hot” and “cold” foods. These qualities indicated not temperature but their effects on the body: for instance, meat, ginger, and fried foods were “heating”; by contrast, cabbage, shellfish, and boiled foods were “cooling.” A person with a fever should eat cooling foods, while a cold sufferer needed heating foods. Grains such as rice and millet were considered neutral. formalized only in the fifth century CE after the arrival of Buddhism, and disagreements remained as to the exact nature of particular foods.Centuries of stability under the Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE) allowed an agricultural revolution. Innovation had begun already in the Eastern Zhou dynasty with the forging of iron plows, and Han officials producedelaborate agricultural manuals and maintained state granaries to prevent famine. search_index.content: Medium The Cognitive Dissonance of Modern Motherhood | by Kerala Goodkin | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Member-only story Parenting Motherhood Work Capitalism Family The Cognitive Dissonance of Modern Motherhood On reconciling my maternal instincts with a world that dismisses and denies them Kerala Goodkin 13 min read · Oct 22, 2024 -- 46 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by deeepblue via Getty Images I feel like an idiot. The HR director at my job has just informed me that there are no paid maternity leave options, but that I’m entitled to 14 weeks of unpaid leave under the FMLA. “Entitled?” I think but do not say aloud. Later, I learn that the law was specifically enacted so that women who take time off to give birth and subsequently care for a newborn don’t lose their jobs. But there is no way we’re going to pay them for that shit. The HR director tells me I also will be “entitled” to six weeks of disability pay, about 60 percent of my paycheck, following the birth of my child. Later, I learn that six weeks is the amount of time that women typically need to physically recover from the act of labor. It has nothing whatsoever to do with the needs of the newborn. When women are no longer “disabled,” of course, they can’t be expected to take free money for just sitting around with a baby. I should have done my research, should have asked these questions sooner. I’m already pregnant, have only meager savings, and can barely afford six weeks at 60 percent pay, not to mention eight subsequent unpaid weeks. Why I Still Crave My Husband After Ten… | by Srujana | Nudge | Nov, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Nudge · Ideas that move you forward Member-only story Marriage Love Obsessions Journey This Happened To Me Only for love: Obsession Why I Still Crave My Husband After Ten Years. The Beautiful Truth of Being Deeply in Love Everyday Srujana 2 min read · 4 days ago -- 4 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Our love painted in everyday moments. AI generated. Every single moment, every single hour, every single day, I want him right beside me. This feeling is not just about physical desire. It is about pure, deep love. I just want to look at him, hold his hand, and cuddle with him. Why do I feel this way? I think it is because his arms are the only truly safe place left for me in this world. A place just for me. But living in a big, joint family makes it hard to find private time. Recently, my husband’s younger brother came to visit. Since our house is crowded and there were no extra rooms, our bedroom was given to him. My husband works late and finishes at 3:00 AM. When he finally got home, we had no choice but to sleep in separate places. Whenever this happens, my heart fills with disappointment. My only wish at night is so simple: to cuddle against his chest while I fall asleep, feel a gentle kiss on my forehead, and hear him softly say good night. That is all I really want. search_index.description: Miles and Memories: Chronicles of Asia Jeju on the Beat: Exploring South Korea’s Island 11/08/2026–11/10/2026 On the way to Jeju, Andrew and I were delayed by a couple of hours. Not a huge deal …
search_index.content: Medium Miles and Memories: Chronicles of Asia | by Samir Naqvi | Nov, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Korea Travel Culture Journey Adventure Miles and Memories: Chronicles of Asia Jeju on the Beat: Exploring South Korea’s Island Samir Naqvi 12 min read · 6 days ago -- 2 Listen Share 11/08/2026–11/10/2026 On the way to Jeju, Andrew and I were delayed by a couple of hours. Not a huge deal, but it kind of derailed our plan for the day, as by the time we got the car, it was already 5 PM and most attractions closed at 6 PM. First Take on Jeju We were staying at the Sheraton Jeju, which I was excited about given they have a guaranteed lounge benefit in Asia. We ended up just heading to the hotel, checking in, and having some champagne and food at the lounge. There was a full beef loin, some shrimp dishes, fried rice, salads, and a huge selection overall. I really enjoyed it, but Andrew had a different take, mentioning that the better the hotel food and benefits are, the less likely you are to go out and explore the local food scene. I don’t know, I don’t think it’s quite that black and white. Press enter or click to view image in full size Press enter or click to view image in full size Press enter or click to view image in full size Sheraton Hotel in Jeju After this, we went to Jeju Dongmun Market, an outdoor market mostly focused on food, but with some shops as well. This area is famous for its citrus, so their fresh juice really slapped. I also finally got to try bingsu, the last Korean food high on my list. I got mango and really liked it. It’s essentially a combination of shaved ice, condensed milk, maybe a bit of ice cream, and fresh mango. They’re also famous for black pork, which I don’t eat, but Andrew tried it and liked it! Press enter or click to view image in full size Press enter or click to view image in full size Press enter or click to view image in full size Press enter or click to view image in full size Press enter or click to view image in full size Dongmun Market: Tried Fresh Orange Juice and Mango Bingsu, both good For the end of the night, it was time to hit the casino, something we thought would be super easy but turned out to be quite the adventure. We started with our hotel, but that casino had been closed for unknown reasons for the past month. Then the one a 10-minute walk away was also closed. At this point, we debated whether we should just go home, but we both wanted to play blackjack, so we ripped it over to Jeju Dream Tower Casino in an Uber. We finally got onto the casino floor, only to find out they had decided there would be no blackjack or roulette that day, just 40 tables of baccarat, which neither of us was interested in. Don’t they want our money? At this point, we were too invested to give up, so we walked another 10 minutes to Paradise Casino, and finally, we found the tables! They gave us a few free credits, and drinks were free, just like in America, which was nice. I played blackjack, roulette, and slots. Slots were really boring, I don’t get the appeal, but I had to burn through the free credits somehow. I ended up leaving up 302,000 KRW, which I was happy with, and Andrew finished up around the same amount. So, after all that running around, a solid run and a good time! I unfortunately didn’t take any photos here, but included some reference. Press enter or click to view image in full size Press enter or click to view image in full size Jeju Dream Tower Casino & Paradise Casino (Stock) Exploring in the Rain Unfortunately, Monday was a bit tough, as most of the appeal of Jeju is outdoors and it was raining the entire day. We tried to do as much as possible, but it just isn’t as fun if you can’t chill in the outdoors. Rain was strong enough that I took an Umbrella and if you know me, you know I don’t believe in umbrellas (its just water). Press enter or click to view image in full size A Rare SIghting We started the day off by driving to Osulloc Tea Museum , which was a massive complex of buildings filled with tourists. They focus on growing tea locally and producing a ton of matcha. The main area had a selection of tea samples, which was nice given the rainy weather, a very large shop, and a cafe. From there, you could walk out to the actual tea fields and have some tea or take photos. Unfortunately, it was raining, so it wasn’t that fantastic, but I could see this being an amazing place in good weather. We had lunch at the sister restaurant there, but the matcha-flavored meals tasted kind of odd. I got a tofu dish that I really didn’t like. I also tried a matcha cake from the main cafe, which was good and had a crepe-style texture, but not as good as Lady M, which makes similar cakes in the US. One hidden highlight was the Tea Stone Cellar, which was off to the side and not really advertised. This was a fancier tea experience where they showed you the process and had someone there to discuss everything with you. It was more immersive and a cool 15-minute experience! Press enter or click to view image in full size Press enter or click to view image in full size Press enter or click to view image in full size Press enter or click to view image in full size Press enter or click to view image in full size Osulloc Tea Museum Next, we went to Cheonjeyeon Waterfalls , where there are three waterfalls and a bridge surrounded by nature. The first one was very close and supposedly only has water during rainfall. Unfortunately, even with all the rain we had, there was nothing there! The second one was super beautiful, while the third, which was quite far away, was a bit underwhelming. Effort-adjusted, it wasn’t great, so many steps. search_index.description: Thomas M. Wells, Donald Trump’s former attorney, revisits his 20 warnings from 2016 and reflects on Trump’s presidency, leadership, character, and American politics.
search_index.content: Medium Donald Trump Hired Me as His Lawyer. Ten Years Later, Here’s What I Got Right. | by Thomas M. Wells | The Political Prism | Oct, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in The Political Prism · Celebrating diverse political perspectives and viewpoints. Society Donald Trump Culture Leadership Politics Donald Trump Hired Me as His Lawyer. Ten Years Later, Here’s What I Got Right. And where I fell short Thomas M. Wells 7 min read · Oct 27, 2026 -- 170 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Image by the author. A nybody who knows me at all knows that I am not a fan of Donald Trump . This is despite the fact that Donald Trump and I go way back. In 1987, we were both still relatively young men. I was thirty-five; he was forty-one. He hired me as a lawyer to represent him on a major real estate project in northern New Jersey. It was a big deal for me. I had only recently started my own law firm, and landing Donald Trump as a client certainly didn’t hurt my career. So perhaps I should feel grateful. Trump, I suspect, would say I should be. I am not. Knowing Trump, I suspected that the campaign was as much about promoting the Trump brand as becoming president. At the time, I was pleased to have such a flashy and prominent client. But from the beginning, I was underwhelmed by the man himself — his over-the-top showmanship, his enormous ego, and the gap between the image he projected and the person I saw up close. Fast forward to 2016. My former client was running for president of the United States. At first, it didn’t seem real. Knowing Trump, I suspected that the campaign was as much about promoting the Trump brand as becoming president. I felt I had to say something. So I sat down and began writing a list of reasons why I believed Donald Trump would make a very bad president. I started with five. Five became ten. Ten became twenty. And each reason came with an argument explaining why I thought it mattered. I sent the resulting essay to my local newspaper and, at the suggestion of a client’s sister who was a good friend of Hillary Clinton, to the Huffington Post . They gave it a much better title than I had: “Donald Trump Hired Me As an Attorney. Please Don’t Support Him For President.” They added some photographs and published it. Then something happened that I never expected. The article went viral and, within a few days, received millions of views. As I recall, the Huffington Post alone showed roughly 39,000 shares and 122,000 likes. The essay was republished, quoted, linked and discussed all over the place. I was stunned. Here is how I began the article: “I like authenticity, especially as compared to survey-tested or heavily spun. I am prepared to let a candidate say something that I don’t completely agree with and still support him or her. I think the need to be politically correct has gone too far. I also think the media often hypes and slants stories to the point of being untruthful. I think a prosperous middle class is the key to the American success story, both economically and politically, and that lobbyists have way too much sway. I am very much a pragmatist, so much so that I like compromise more than I like ideology. I like deals, especially those that are win-win. So Donald Trump is my candidate, right? He is NOT!” I then explained the legal work I had taken on: obtaining approvals for a major northern New Jersey shopping mall, hotel and office building that like so many Trump projects was going to bear his name: Trump Centre. Getting those approvals would not be easy. Nonetheless, I was thrilled to get the assignment. This was long before Apprentice and other TV fame, but Trump was already a celebrity businessman. He had completed Trump Tower and had an impressive office, a yacht, helicopters, and casinos, with an airline shuttle following soon. From a distance, he looked enormously successful. Up close, I began seeing something different. One incident has stayed with me for nearly forty years. Trump, a couple of others and I were riding in a limousine to meet with the editorial board of a New Jersey newspaper. My married client decided to regale me with stories about the number and quality of young women who, in his words, “want me.” I was shocked and uncomfortable. To my embarrassment now, I admit that I kept smiling and laughing. I was a young lawyer, and I wanted and needed this very important client to be happy. Another exchange was less offensive but perhaps even more revealing. At the time, newspaper and magazine stories regularly described the Trump family’s private apartment in Trump Tower. Depending on which story you read, it had eight rooms, sixteen rooms, twenty rooms, maybe thirty. I was curious, so one day, riding up in the elevator together, I asked Trump how many rooms the apartment actually had. I have never forgotten his answer: “However many they will print.” Truth wasn’t the point. Image was. In my 2016 article, I summed up the Trump I had known this way: “Donald Trump was then, as he is now, larger than life, particularly in his own eyes, and at the same time frighteningly small with very little moral grounding. He was then, and still is, all ego and show.” That was my assessment in 2016. It is now 2026. In the intervening decade, Donald Trump has won the presidency twice, lost it once, been impeached twice, faced criminal prosecutions and a criminal conviction, transformed the Republican Party, returned to the White House, and altered American politics in ways that will be debated for decades. Today I want to look again at the twenty warnings I wrote before any of that happened. How did they hold up? Remarkably well, I think. Those warnings were about his fitness for office, however, not his ability to win it. He won twice, so obviously my warnings did not work. I underestimated the consequences of putting his character, temperament and worldview at the center of American political life

It Didn’t Make the Next Part Easy | by Erik Blair | Oct, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Mastodon Member-only story Thailand Culture Dating Lifestyle Life Lessons Thailand Made It Easy to Meet Women After 60. It Didn’t Make the Next Part Easy Where older foreign men really meet Thai women, what each side actually wants, which myths are myths, where the fraud runs in both directions, and why the where was never the hard part. Erik Blair 16 min read · Oct 31, 2026 -- 26 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Image created by eloquent AI prompt engineering Saturday, half past five, the corner coffee shop across from the Wua Lai walking street. The chair is mine. Everyone says so, the Thai staff and the farang regulars both, and they say it like an accusation. The couples I know go past this corner all week. Tom and Ploy, tandem on one motorbike, on their way to yoga or a hike. Pete and his wife, on the days she isn’t at the farm. Dev and Nan used to pass every morning on the way to the gym, until they didn’t. Walter has never once brought his wife by. In two years I have never seen her. Read this story for free here . Not one of them met on the walking street. Nobody does. So where? It took me two years here to learn that the question has an answer, and that the answer is the least interesting part of the story. Thomas Oppong 9 min read · Nov 5, 2026 -- 22 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by Maxence Amé on Unsplash History has a habit of celebrating the same names. Einstein. Newton. Leonardo da Vinci. Aristotle. Of course, they deserve their reputations. But some of the most interesting lessons for living, thinking and achieving your great things come from people whose names you probably don’t know. I didn’t know many of the brilliant minds in this essay before my research. Now, I know. Take Mary Anning, for example. In 1811, at 12, she came across something extraordinary in Lyme Regis, England. Her brother Joseph had discovered a huge fossilised skull in the cliffs. Mary spent months carefully excavating the rest of the skeleton. The discovery would go on to be recognised as one of the first major fossils. It belonged to an extinct marine reptile that lived millions of years before humans. But Mary wasn’t a professor. She didn’t have a prestigious scientific education. She came from a poor family. She had to sell fossils to help support them. She taught herself geology and anatomy, made important discoveries, and became a trusted expert among some of the leading scientists of her time. There was just one problem. Many of the men who benefited from her discoveries received the recognition she didn’t. Member-only story Life Self Improvement Mindfulness Personal Development Life Lessons I realised that people’s toxic traits are the opposite of their love languages And once you see it, you can’t unsee it Sadhvi Pharasi 4 min read · Oct 9, 2026 -- 49 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by Gwyn Hay on Unsplash Not a Medium member? Read this story here . I was sitting with a friend who’d just gotten off the phone with her mother. It was one of those calls that leaves you holding the device like it bit you. And she said, “She knows exactly what to say to just…destroy me.” And I asked something that I thought was obvious but apparently wasn’t: “Is she also the person who knows exactly what to say to make you feel loved?” Long pause. “Yeah. She is.” The person who builds you up with words is the same person who knows where to aim them when they want to tear you down. I’ve been watching this pattern for a while now. So, someone whose love language is quality time, who shows love by being present, by giving you their full attention, by sitting with you and making you feel like the only person in the room? Their toxic move is withdrawal. Silent treatment. Disappearing. They don’t yell. They remove the thing they know you value most, which is them showing up. And it works very well in their favour because it’s the inversion of how they made you feel loved. The warmth was real. The cold is just as real. search_index.description: Every person you meet carries a different version of you in their mind Sometimes, we wonder how others perceive us. Perhaps we all want to be seen as nice, kind, or any other words associated with …
search_index.content: Medium Every person you meet carries a different version of you in their mind | by Devina | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Devina Giving you my unprofessional advice (please take everything with a grain of salt) Press enter or click to view image in full size Source: https://pin.it/65PoHONQS Life Self Improvement Psychology Mental Health This Happened To Me Every person you meet carries a different version of you in their mind Devina 3 min read · Jun 1, 2026 -- 584 Listen Share Sometimes, we wonder how others perceive us. Perhaps we all want to be seen as nice, kind, or any other words associated with positive traits. And to be perceived the way we want, we often become extremely careful about how we carry ourselves in society. We measure every interaction. We curate the stories we choose to tell so we won’t be labeled “too much” and we restrain ourselves from doing something silly because we fear being seen as weird. But no matter how carefully you present yourself, there will always be someone who misunderstands you. Someone might think you are shy simply because you are the quietest person in the room. But maybe you are dealing with personal struggles and still choosing to show up, while all you are really doing is being observant. Someone might see you as lonely because you are not married at the age you are “supposed” to be (according to society’s timeline). What they do not know is that you are enjoying your singleness and you are surrounded by good people who make you feel loved. However, there are also people who are inspired by your hard work and touched by your kindness. Then, they tell you how much your existence matters in their lives. People hold different versions of you. Most of the time, their understanding of you is shaped by limited interactions and specific situations. Instead of trying to change people’s opinions about you, use them as an opportunity to understand yourself better. When someone says you are annoying, you can reflect on the situations in which they felt that way and assess yourself. However, that does not mean you should immediately blame yourself and think, “Oh, I shouldn’t speak too much!” Because whatever labels people place on you do not reflect who you are as a person. You are not defined by those perceptions, but rather by how you grow as a human being. The way you change your views or outgrow versions of yourself that no longer align with what you believe. Most importantly, by the way you remain your authentic self, not performing for others just to gain their approval. You don’t have to explain yourself every time someone misunderstands you. Sometimes, it’s useless. Even when you have grown into a different version of yourself, some old school friends might be surprised and say, “Oh, you’re not that shy kid anymore?” They only know the old version of you that still exists in their minds. They forget that people can change. Their opinions of you are not in your control and no matter how hard you try, there is no guarantee that they will change them. If you crave being seen as good and becoming everyone’s favorite, let me tell you this: it’s a myth. No matter how genuine you try to be, there will always be someone who interprets you the wrong way. Even when you believe you are doing what must be done, some people may still see you as the villain. Don’t shrink yourself just to fit into their comfort or to make sure people get the right idea of you. It is such a waste of energy when you have countless responsibilities in life that truly matter. Let people perceive you however they want. Perhaps that is the price you pay for being seen and building human connection. But you can play your part; to live unapologetically and hold firmly to the values you believe in. In short, whatever people think about you, let them live with those thoughts. Food Sushi Travel Trip Journey A World Cuisine Tour: Unforgettable Dining Experiences Enes Yildirim 3 min read · Feb 18, 2024 -- 2 Listen Share E mbark on a gastronomic journey that takes you around the globe, from the bustling streets of Bangkok to the serene landscapes of Tuscany. This article is your guide to discovering some of the most unforgettable dining experiences that offer not just a meal, but a dive into the depths of local culture and tradition. Perfect for food lovers and adventurous eaters, our world cuisine tour highlights local delicacies, unique dining settings, and culinary practices that define the essence of each destination. Experiencing Asia: A Blend of Tradition and Innovation Tokyo, Japan: A Sushi Odyssey In Tokyo, sushi is not just food; it’s an art form. Visit the world-renowned Tsukiji Market, where the freshest catch of the day becomes exquisite sushi and sashimi pieces. For an unforgettable experience, reserve a seat at one of Tokyo’s Michelin-starred sushi restaurants, where master chefs craft each piece with precision and care. Bangkok, Thailand: Street Food Galore Bangkok’s street food scene is a sensory overload. From spicy pad thai and savory grilled meats to sweet mango sticky rice, the flavors are as vibrant as the city itself. Don’t miss the chance to explore the bustling markets and street food stalls for an authentic taste of Thai cuisine. Journey Through Europe: Culinary Richness and Diversity Tuscany, Italy: A Rustic Feast Tuscany offers a rustic dining experience amidst rolling hills and vineyards. Indulge in traditional dishes like ribollita (bread soup) and bistecca alla fiorentina (Florentine steak). A visit to a local winery for a wine tasting paired with artisanal cheeses and cured meats is a must. Paris, France: Gourmet Delights Paris is synonymous with gourmet cuisine. From cozy bistros serving classic French dishes to high-end restaurants offering innovative gastronomic creations, Paris caters to all palates. Don’t forget to savor a freshly baked croissant or a delicate macaron from a Parisian patisserie. Exploring the Americas: A Melting Pot of Flavors Oaxaca, Mexico: A Taste of Tradition Oaxaca is the heart of Mexican gastronomy. Its markets are filled with indigenous ingredients that make up dishes like mole negro and tlayudas. Participate in a cooking class to learn the secrets of Oaxacan cuisine and the importance of corn, beans, and chili peppers in Mexican culture. New Orleans, USA: The Soul of American Cuisine New Orleans is a melting pot of French, African, and American cultures, reflected in its unique cuisine. Enjoy Creole classics like gumbo and jambalaya, and don’t miss the chance to try a beignet at Café du Monde. The city’s jazz clubs offer the perfect backdrop for a night of dining and music. A Feast for the Senses A world cuisine tour is more than a quest for new flavors; it’s an exploration of the world’s cultural diversity through its culinary traditions. Each destination offers a unique dining experience that tells the story of its people, history, and landscape. So, pack your appetite and set off on a journey that promises unforgettable dining experiences at every turn. Remember, the essence of travel and dining is not just in the tasting but in experiencing the world with all your senses. Whether it’s the spicy aroma of a Thai market, the sound of a Japanese sushi knife, or the sight of an Italian vineyard at sunset, these are the moments that make for a truly unforgettable gastronomic journey. search_index.content: Medium Exotic Encounters: Responsible Tourism in the Wild | by Enes Yildirim | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Mastodon Tourism Animals Nature Travel Wildlife Exotic Encounters: Responsible Tourism in the Wild Enes Yildirim 3 min read · Feb 19, 2024 -- 2 Listen Share In the heart of the untamed wilderness, where the whispers of nature speak volumes, lies the thrilling experience of meeting exotic animals. This encounter, though exhilarating, carries with it a profound responsibility. “Exotic Encounters: Responsible Tourism in the Wild” delves into the ethical engagement with wildlife, ensuring that our pursuit of adventure respects the natural habitat and conserves the biodiversity of our planet. Embracing Responsible Tourism Responsible tourism is not merely a concept but a call to action for travelers seeking encounters with exotic animals. It emphasizes minimal environmental impact, supports wildlife conservation, and promotes the well-being of local communities. When embarking on a journey into the wild, it is crucial to choose tours and experiences that adhere to ethical practices. Look for certifications and endorsements from recognized conservation organizations to ensure that your adventure contributes positively to the environment. The Impact of Human Interaction Human interaction with wildlife can have profound effects, both positive and negative. While well-managed encounters can aid in conservation efforts and foster a deeper appreciation for nature, irresponsible tourism can threaten animal populations and disrupt delicate ecosystems. It’s essential to maintain a respectful distance, refrain from feeding or touching wildlife, and follow the guidance of knowledgeable guides who prioritize animal welfare. Key Destinations for Ethical Wildlife Encounters Globally, there are numerous destinations renowned for ethical wildlife tourism. The Galapagos Islands offer a unique opportunity to observe endemic species in a protected environment. In Africa, safari experiences in Serengeti National Park and the Maasai Mara Reserve are conducted with a deep respect for the natural habitats of majestic creatures like lions, elephants, and giraffes. Closer to the water, the Great Barrier Reef provides a breathtaking view of marine biodiversity, with eco-friendly snorkeling tours that respect the ocean’s fragile ecosystems. Contributing to Conservation Efforts Choosing responsible wildlife encounters also means contributing to conservation efforts. Many ethical tour operators allocate a portion of their proceeds to wildlife protection programs, habitat restoration, and community education projects. By selecting these experiences, tourists play a vital role in the ongoing efforts to preserve the planet’s exotic animals and their habitats. The Role of Education in Responsible Wildlife Tourism Education is a powerful tool in promoting responsible wildlife tourism. Understanding the behaviors, needs, and threats facing exotic animals empowers travelers to make informed decisions. Before embarking on your journey, research the species you hope to encounter and the challenges they face. This knowledge not only enhances your experience but also contributes to a greater awareness of the importance of conservation. M eeting exotic animals in their natural habitats is an unforgettable experience that comes with significant responsibility. By embracing the principles of responsible tourism, we can ensure that our encounters with the wild contribute to the preservation of nature’s wonders for generations to come. Let us tread lightly on the earth, with respect for the magnificent creatures that call it home. search_index.content: Medium Athens: A Blend of Ancient and Modern | by Enes Yildirim | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Mastodon Travel Athens Tourism Tours And Travels Gui̇de Athens: A Blend of Ancient and Modern Enes Yildirim 3 min read · Feb 20, 2024 -- 8 Listen Share A thens, the historical and cultural capital of Greece, is a city steeped in history located on the shores of the Aegean Sea. Known as the birthplace of ancient Greek civilization, this city exudes an atmosphere filled with history at every corner. On my recent trip, I embarked on a journey to explore Athens, and I couldn’t help but be enchanted by this unique experience. Journey to the Acropolis: Upon arriving in Athens, my first stop was, of course, the Acropolis. This ancient citadel, a symbol of Greece, is perched atop a high hill and greets visitors with the splendor of the Parthenon Temple. As I ascended to the Acropolis, walking among the historical ruins, I felt the excitement of traversing through time. Rediscovering the captivating beauty of the ancient era against the backdrop of the city’s panoramic views filled me with profound admiration. Plaka District: Descending from the Acropolis, I visited the heart of the city, known as the Plaka District. With its narrow cobblestone streets, colorful shops, and traditional taverns, Plaka is one of the liveliest and most charming neighborhoods in Athens. Here, while savoring local delicacies, I found myself immersed in a unique blend of ancient and modern atmospheres. Ancient Agora and Old Town: To delve deeper into Athens’ historical fabric, I made my way to the Ancient Agora. This was the place where philosophers like Socrates and Plato once walked. Roaming among the ruins of the Agora felt like embarking on a journey through the past. Afterwards, getting lost in the narrow streets of the Old Town and wandering among the traditional houses made me feel as if time stood still. Modern Athens: Athens not only boasts the legacy of ancient times but also thrives as a modern city. Central points like Monastiraki Square and Syntagma Square are lined with modern cafes, restaurants, and shopping centers. Exploring these areas allowed me to discover the modern and dynamic side of the city. As I strolled through the streets of Athens, I savored the experience of exploring a city intertwined with history. Following the footsteps of ancient Greek civilization while experiencing the vibrant atmosphere of a modern capital was an unforgettable experience. Athens was not just a trip for me; it was a journey through time. A bridge between the past and the future was built before my eyes, and this experience will forever leave a lasting impression on me. search_index.content: Medium To The Smelly Woman In 5B. You don’t know me, but thank you. | by Greyson Ferguson | The Memoirist | Oct, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in The Memoirist · We exclusively publish memoirs: The creative stories unpacked from the nostalgic hope chests of our lives. Member-only story Memoir Travel Memories Sex Travel Writing To The Smelly Woman In 5B You don’t know me, but thank you. Greyson Ferguson 6 min read · Oct 30, 2026 -- 53 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by Nirmal Rajendharkumar on Unsplash 5C. The flight attendant scanned my paper boarding pass, welcomed me aboard with a tired smile, then turned to the next passenger. Walking the boarding ramp, a woman in line snapped a selfie, her lips puckering as wide as the peace sign she flashed. Behind her, the jet’s Rolls-Royce engine and neon-vested workers were likely caught in her photo. The walkway swayed, and I visualized the tunnel cracking like an egg before crashing to the tarmac. Force of habit. Ever since seeing an oblivious mom clap her hands as her small boy fiddled with the boarding ramp’s control joystick, my mind immediately feared the worst. There were no children playing with ramp controls today. Just a line of passengers. I pulled out my passport and scanned the folded-in ticket. 5C. I knew the seat. I’d checked a dozen times since the check-in kiosk vomited out the tracing-paper-thin boarding pass. A force of habit. The onboard attendant offered a Xeroxed smile as I sideled to my seat. What was it again? 5C. The first row of premium economy behind first class. I stuffed my carry-on into the overhead compartment and took my seat next to the window. What Went Wrong – and What Collectors Check Now | by Anon NFTs | Oct, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Anon NFTs Anon NFT have collection that are all liquidity backed on liquid platform . https://anonnfts.com info@anonnfts.com https://liquidnfts.finance/ To buy Artificial Intelligence Bitcoin Blockchain Cryptocurrency Nft Why Did NFTs Crash? What Went Wrong – and What Collectors Check Now Anon NFTs 7 min read · Oct 27, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size The hype faded. The record didn’t. Why NFTs crashed and what collectors check now. An honest look at why NFTs flopped after 2021, whether NFTs are dead, and what has changed since. Published by Anon NFTs – https://anonnfts.com 27 October 2026 Why did NFTs crash? If you remember 2021, you remember the headlines. Digital art selling at Christie’s. Profile pictures changing hands for the price of a house. Then, almost as quickly, the noise faded, prices fell and a lot of collections went quiet. So what actually went wrong? And are NFTs dead, or did something more useful survive the crash? This piece is an honest answer, written by a small NFT project that is still building, one public day at a time. Let’s break it down. Why Did NFTs Crash? Many 2021 collections were priced on hype, with all the mint money going to creators and nothing held behind the NFTs. When new buyers stopped arriving, prices fell and some projects walked away. That’s partly why some marketplaces now hold part of each mint on-chain as liquidity against the collection. That’s the short version. The longer version has a few parts, and none of them is about the technology itself. An NFT is just a unique record on a blockchain that shows who owns a specific item. That record still works exactly as it did in 2021. What changed was the story people were told about it. What Went Wrong With NFTs? Five Honest Reasons Reason one: prices were built on the next buyer For most NFTs, the only thing holding the price up was the belief that someone else would pay more later. That works while new people keep arriving. When they stop, there is nothing underneath, and the price can fall a long way, sometimes to nothing. Reason two: the mint money left the building On a typical mint, the money went straight to the creator. That’s fair enough for art. But it meant the NFT itself held nothing once the sale cleared, so holders had no figure to look at other than the last sale price. Reason three: promises replaced proof Roadmaps promised games, metaverses and communities. Some were delivered. Many weren’t. When a project’s value rests on promises, every missed deadline chips away at trust, and there’s no record to check. Reason four: scams and rug pulls Fake mint links, wallet-draining signatures and teams that disappeared with the money all damaged trust in the whole space, including honest projects. If you want to know the warning signs, our guide on spotting a rug pull covers them: https://anonnfts.com/spot-a-rug-pull Reason five: the floor price told only half the story People watched the floor price as if it were a value. It isn’t. The floor is just the lowest asking price right now, and a few cheap listings can move it. When everyone watches one fragile number, panic spreads fast. More on that here: https://anonnfts.com/floor-price-explained Are NFTs Dead in 2026? Not dead, but much quieter than in 2021. At the time of writing, trading volumes are far below the peak and many old collections have no buyers. Activity continues in gaming, art, tickets and backed collections with on-chain records. Judge any project by what you can check, not by hype. That’s the part the crash headlines tend to miss. The hype collapsed. The technology didn’t. If you’re curious how we got here, our history of profile-picture NFTs tells the story from the early experiments to today: https://anonnfts.com/pfp-nft-history Myth vs Fact: What the NFT Crash Did and Didn’t Prove Myth: “The crash proved NFTs are worthless.” Fact: It proved that NFTs with nothing behind them depend entirely on demand. That’s a lesson about design, not a verdict on every NFT that will ever exist. Myth: “A low floor price means a project has failed.” Fact: A floor price shows what sellers are asking. It says nothing on its own about the project’s activity, its record or what, if anything, is held behind each NFT. Myth: “Backing means an NFT can’t lose value.” Fact: Liquidity-backed does not mean risk-free. Backing is a record of what’s held under a platform’s rules. Tokens can move, fees apply, smart contracts carry risk, and resale prices are still set by buyers. What Changed After the NFT Crash? The most useful change is that some projects and marketplaces now show something you can check instead of something you have to believe. One example is the Liquid NFT Marketplace: https://liquidnfts.finance According to its published fee structure ( https://liquidnfts.finance/about ), at the time of writing, these are the fees. On a new mint, at least 50% of the price is added to that NFT’s liquidity, 40% goes to the creator, 5% to Liquid and 5% to the liquidity of existing NFTs on the platform. On a resale or redemption, 20% is charged in total: 10% to the creator, 5% to liquidity and 5% to Liquid, so the seller or redeemer receives 80%. Liquidity is held in FUSD, and the marketplace runs on Polygon, Ethereum, BNB Chain and BESC. That design answers reason two directly. Part of the mint money stays with the NFT, and anyone can see it on-chain. It also means every collection’s activity adds a little to the others, which is why we cheer on every collection on Liquid, from Liquid Apes to the Liquid Genesis Collection. It’s one option among many marketplaces, each with its own strengths. Whichever you use, the same rule applies: check, don’t trust. Other Project — https://coincodecap.com/ & Email — gaurav@coincodecap.com Member-only story Bitcoin Cryptocurrency Crypto Gold Money Gold, Silver, or Bitcoin: Which Store of Value Wins the Next Decade? Chetan Dugar 10 min read · Nov 6, 2026 -- 4 Listen Share All three just failed the same exam. I priced them in each other, timed fifty years of crashes, checked who buys at the bottom, and made a call for 2036. Press enter or click to view image in full size Three ways to know its real Drop a real silver coin on a hard table and it rings. A clean, high note that hangs in the air for a second. Coin dealers have trusted that sound for centuries. A fake just thuds. Gold has its own test. Its so heavy for its size that you feel a real coin in your palm before you look at it. Bitcoin makes no sound at all. Your phone checks the math in silence and tells you its real. Three tests, three kinds of trust. And right now all three are failing the same exam. Gold is down about 28% from its January record. Silver is down almost 60%. Bitcoin is down almost 40% from its peak a year ago. If you bought any of the world’s favourite stores of value at the top, what you stored was a loss. So which one would you trust with the next ten years of your savings? Gold, silver or Bitcoin? Pick one now. Mine comes near the end, along with the numbers that argue against it. Written by Chetan Dugar 1.3K followers · 15 following Founder of Xtin Capital. search_index.content: Medium The Orthoverse: Rebooted. We’re back and we’re still doomed | by Keir Finlow-Bates | Nov, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Metaverse Voxel Luanti Nft The Orthoverse: Rebooted Keir Finlow-Bates 6 min read · 5 days ago -- Listen Share We’re back and we’re still doomed What could be more dooming than being doomed? Returning to be doomed again! And so, I’m glad to announce that the Orthoverse is back. The Lore In 2022, Richard Piacentini (the Other Guy) and I got sucked down an NFT/metaverse rabbit hole, starting with the release of a non-fungible token contract in which every wallet got airdropped one of the tokens . We decided to run with it, and as a side-hobby ended up with a voxel-based metaverse built on a rickety collection of adapted open-source JavaScript packages . Not because either of us was particularly taken with the idea that everyone would eventually be spending half their life in a Neal Stephenson Snow Crash-inspired virtual world, or that a blocky brightly colored world was the way to go to achieve that goal, but simply because it was fun. By NFT project standards it was a roaring success, falling comfortably in the top 1% of token collections based on profits and transaction volume. Just short of 2000 tokens were activated, and we made a small five-figure income, which was all blown on a contract migration to fix a bug, and legal and accounting fees. Then the craze (and it was a craze) passed, everyone lost interest, and we moved on to other things. But while it lasted, we had a small, passionate … not passionate, but definitely amused … community of enthusiasts. Our own culture and traditions grew, and the whole thing was a great learning experience. The First Doom The original Orthoverse died a slow heat-death. Bugs were uncovered that needed fixing, but for which I didn’t have the motivation. Domain renewal fees weren’t paid. And then a disk crash wiped out the final remnants. As a result, in early 2025 the Orthoverse was nothing but a single smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain. All the support infrastructure — the web interface, the world database, and the voxel game: gone. For good, or so I thought. The Change Things have moved on a lot since 2022, through the advent of AI-assisted coding. Or indeed since 2025, when Cursor AI added fallback eval() statements to an API it was asked to write (this means that the AI wrote code that said “If I receive some code over the internet, even if it’s malware, run it on this machine.”) Back at the beginning of this decade I was able to write code that did what I wanted by hand, but it took a lot of time. These days I work with LLMs, and progress for proof-of-concept implementations is amazingly fast. I find the experience of working with an LLM is far, far better than my previous experiences with hired contractor programming teams. It costs $30 a month rather than $5 or $10 thousand, I get immediate feedback, and quite frankly, the results are more robust and look better. What it does require, is the development of a new kind of knowledge. Different things go wrong. It is a bit like managing a team of idiot-savants who know of the existence of almost everything, but the meaning of nothing. And I have gained this knowledge by running trivial little side-projects, partly for enjoyment, and partly to gain more and more agent assisted coding experience and to keep up with new developments and improvement. Because the AI world changes fast. The Reboot When I first kicked off coding up the Orthoverse, picking which platform, which engine, and which programming language to use required extensive research. Searching through Stack Overflow answers, going down dead-ends in out-of-date, inaccurate, or just plain wrong Medium articles, and stuff like that. With an LLM like Claude, all that data is distilled into one place, and is semantically searchable. When I asked it, “What’s a good voxel engine to use for re-implementing this,” pointing it at the JavaScript Orthoverse repositories, it suggested Luanti as a good fit, and it was right. When I pointed out that I don’t know Lua and didn’t want to learn it, it suggested that it write the code, and I test it. That got me hooked on this latest project. Then there was the writing of code, unit testing it, and running the whole lot with a full walk-through each time. Four years ago a simple feature like generative art heraldic crests took an entire weekend. Now it was just two prompts. And so for the last few weeks, all I have had to do is take a five minute break from work every hour to look at the latest response, make a few decisions, provide some more descriptions and opinions, and the LLM has done the rest. That meant that all the ideas I had in my head, but never got around to implementing in the Orthoverse version 1, could be spun up as a side-thought. Getting the Orthoverse version 2 to the same state and stability as version one took about five days in real time, with four hours of real effort. The New Stuff mobs: the LLM generates passable skins for new monsters like zombies, kobolds, warlocks, and will-o’-the-wisps. a voxel-game combat system based on what I dimly remember from Ultima Underworld (a 1990s role-playing game): hold to charge your blow, and different weapon types with different ranges, recovery times, damage, and effectiveness against different monsters. For example, a feature like “make a dagger feeble when used front-on, but far more deadly when used to stab a monster in the back.” Press enter or click to view image in full size The weapons are shown in the characters’ hands, and move appropriately when wielded. adventures and interactive puzzles: these are more effort, typically requiring six or seven prompts, but that includes taking a basic idea and getting the LLM to help expand it into something akin to a D&D module. What Went Wrong – and What Collectors Check Now Anon NFTs 7 min read · Oct 27, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size The hype faded. The record didn’t. Why NFTs crashed and what collectors check now. An honest look at why NFTs flopped after 2021, whether NFTs are dead, and what has changed since. Published by Anon NFTs – https://anonnfts.com 27 October 2026 Why did NFTs crash? If you remember 2021, you remember the headlines. Digital art selling at Christie’s. Profile pictures changing hands for the price of a house. Then, almost as quickly, the noise faded, prices fell and a lot of collections went quiet. So what actually went wrong? And are NFTs dead, or did something more useful survive the crash? This piece is an honest answer, written by a small NFT project that is still building, one public day at a time. Let’s break it down. Why Did NFTs Crash? Many 2021 collections were priced on hype, with all the mint money going to creators and nothing held behind the NFTs. When new buyers stopped arriving, prices fell and some projects walked away. That’s partly why some marketplaces now hold part of each mint on-chain as liquidity against the collection. That’s the short version. The longer version has a few parts, and none of them is about the technology itself. An NFT is just a unique record on a blockchain that shows who owns a specific item. That record still works exactly as it did in 2021. What changed was the story people were told about it. What Went Wrong With NFTs? Five Honest Reasons Reason one: prices were built on the next buyer For most NFTs, the only thing holding the price up was the belief that someone else would pay more later. That works while new people keep arriving. When they stop, there is nothing underneath, and the price can fall a long way, sometimes to nothing. Reason two: the mint money left the building On a typical mint, the money went straight to the creator. That’s fair enough for art. But it meant the NFT itself held nothing once the sale cleared, so holders had no figure to look at other than the last sale price. Reason three: promises replaced proof Roadmaps promised games, metaverses and communities. Some were delivered. Many weren’t. When a project’s value rests on promises, every missed deadline chips away at trust, and there’s no record to check. Reason four: scams and rug pulls Fake mint links, wallet-draining signatures and teams that disappeared with the money all damaged trust in the whole space, including honest projects. If you want to know the warning signs, our guide on spotting a rug pull covers them: https://anonnfts.com/spot-a-rug-pull Reason five: the floor price told only half the story People watched the floor price as if it were a value. It isn’t. The floor is just the lowest asking price right now, and a few cheap listings can move it. When everyone watches one fragile number, panic spreads fast. More on that here: https://anonnfts.com/floor-price-explained Are NFTs Dead in 2026? Not dead, but much quieter than in 2021. At the time of writing, trading volumes are far below the peak and many old collections have no buyers. Activity continues in gaming, art, tickets and backed collections with on-chain records. Judge any project by what you can check, not by hype. That’s the part the crash headlines tend to miss. The hype collapsed. The technology didn’t. If you’re curious how we got here, our history of profile-picture NFTs tells the story from the early experiments to today: https://anonnfts.com/pfp-nft-history Myth vs Fact: What the NFT Crash Did and Didn’t Prove Myth: “The crash proved NFTs are worthless.” Fact: It proved that NFTs with nothing behind them depend entirely on demand. That’s a lesson about design, not a verdict on every NFT that will ever exist. Myth: “A low floor price means a project has failed.” Fact: A floor price shows what sellers are asking. It says nothing on its own about the project’s activity, its record or what, if anything, is held behind each NFT. Myth: “Backing means an NFT can’t lose value.” Fact: Liquidity-backed does not mean risk-free. Backing is a record of what’s held under a platform’s rules. Tokens can move, fees apply, smart contracts carry risk, and resale prices are still set by buyers. What Changed After the NFT Crash? The most useful change is that some projects and marketplaces now show something you can check instead of something you have to believe. One example is the Liquid NFT Marketplace: https://liquidnfts.finance According to its published fee structure ( https://liquidnfts.finance/about ), at the time of writing, these are the fees. On a new mint, at least 50% of the price is added to that NFT’s liquidity, 40% goes to the creator, 5% to Liquid and 5% to the liquidity of existing NFTs on the platform. On a resale or redemption, 20% is charged in total: 10% to the creator, 5% to liquidity and 5% to Liquid, so the seller or redeemer receives 80%. Liquidity is held in FUSD, and the marketplace runs on Polygon, Ethereum, BNB Chain and BESC. That design answers reason two directly. Part of the mint money stays with the NFT, and anyone can see it on-chain. It also means every collection’s activity adds a little to the others, which is why we cheer on every collection on Liquid, from Liquid Apes to the Liquid Genesis Collection. It’s one option among many marketplaces, each with its own strengths. Whichever you use, the same rule applies: check, don’t trust. search_index.content: Medium What is an NFT token ID? The number that tells one NFT from every other | by Anon NFTs | Nov, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Anon NFTs Anon NFT have collection that are all liquidity backed on liquid platform . https://anonnfts.com info@anonnfts.com https://liquidnfts.finance/ To buy Blockchain Bitcoin Cryptocurrency Defi Nft What is an NFT token ID? The number that tells one NFT from every other Anon NFTs 5 min read · 6 days ago -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Three ANON figures, three numbers: each NFT is told apart by its token ID. Published by Anon NFTs – AnonNfts.com 10 November 2026 An NFT token ID is the number a smart contract gives each token it creates. Together with the contract address, it points to one specific NFT and no other. If you know both, you can look that NFT up on-chain and see who holds it. Think of the contract address as a street and the token ID as a house number. “Number 12" means nothing on its own, but “12 Oak Lane” is one front door. That pairing is the whole idea, so let’s take it apart. Why do you need the contract address as well as the token ID? Every collection has its own contract, and most of them start counting from 0 or 1. So thousands of different NFTs share the token ID 1. Only the pair is unique. “Token 1 in contract A” and “token 1 in contract B” are completely different items, owned by different people, with different histories. This matters for safety. A copycat collection can use the same name, the same artwork and the same numbers. What it cannot copy is the original contract address. If the address does not match the one on the project’s official website, it is not the same NFT, whatever the number says. So where do you actually find these two pieces? Where can you find an NFT’s token ID? Most marketplaces show it on the NFT’s own page, often in a section called “Details” or “Blockchain details”. You will usually see the contract address, the token ID, the token standard and the blockchain listed together. Your wallet may show it too. Open the NFT inside the wallet app and look for a details or info tab. The NFT’s name often includes a number, such as “#57". That is usually the token ID, but not always. The name comes from the project’s metadata, so treat it as a label and confirm the real token ID in the details. Once you have the number, it unlocks more than ownership. What does a token ID connect to? On a contract that follows the ERC-721 standard, described here: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-721, each token ID has exactly one owner at a time. The contract can answer “who owns token 57?” through a function called ownerOf. Many contracts also offer a tokenURI function. Give it the token ID and it returns a link to that token’s metadata: its name, description, image and traits. So the token ID is the key that joins the on-chain record to the picture you see. The image file usually sits somewhere else, but the ID tells you which one belongs to which token. That leads to a common question about the numbers themselves. Does a low token ID make an NFT worth more? Not by itself. A low number only shows the order in which tokens were created, and some contracts do not even number them in order. Some buyers like early or “neat” numbers, but that is a preference, not a rule. It does not set a resale price, and resale prices can fall below what you paid. On backed marketplaces, figures can also be tracked token by token. Before buying, check the details for the exact token ID you are looking at, not a similar one from the same collection. Now for the quick ones. Quick questions Can a token ID change? No. Once a token is minted, its ID stays the same for its whole life, even when it moves between wallets. What happens to the token ID if an NFT is burned? The token is removed from circulation. Its ID normally is not handed to a new token, although that depends on the contract. Are token IDs the same on every blockchain? No. A token ID only has meaning inside its own contract on its own chain, so always note the chain as well. Is a token ID the same as a transaction hash? No. The hash identifies one transaction, such as a mint or a transfer. The token ID identifies the NFT itself. Here is how to check all of this without connecting anything. How can you check it yourself? Start from the project’s official website and open the collection through its link. Note the blockchain, the contract address and the token ID from the NFT’s details. Paste the contract address into the matching block explorer. For Polygon, that is https://polygonscan.com. Search for the token ID, or open the contract’s read-only tools and try ownerOf with that number. The answer should match the wallet shown on the marketplace. Then look at the token’s transfer history. You should see when it was minted and every wallet it has passed through. Reading these pages needs no wallet connection and no signature. If a site asks you to approve a transaction just to look, close it. Check it on-chain, then decide for yourself.
