I Looked. Here’s the Truth. Did Stanford just release something that destroys ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini? Because that’s what I’m seeing everywhere online. Gursimar Singh 12 min read · Oct 31, 2026 -- 49 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Like this one chart that’s doing the rounds. Hard Sudoku. A small AI built the ChatGPT way solves about 1 in 100 puzzles. A small AI built with this new thing called NCM solves 86 in 100. Look, you’re going to hear this kind of stuff all the time. We’re used to it now. Every week there’s a new model and it’s better than the rest. But there is something different about this one. NCM isn’t just a new model. It’s a new way of building one. And I’ll be honest, there’s a real reason people are excited. It does something ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini physically can’t do. It goes back and fixes what it already wrote. But before we get to that, you need to know how today’s AI actually writes. Because once you get that, everything else clicks. How ChatGPT really writes (this surprised me) When you ask ChatGPT a question, it doesn’t give you the answer all at once. It writes one word at a time. Here’s the Fast, Clean One Forget clever prompts. Here’s the ultimate hands-on guide to AI coding productivity, with insights you won’t find anywhere else Jose Crespo, PhD 14 min read · Oct 30, 2026 -- 121 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size The Mythical Man-Month Meets the Mythical 10x AI Developer If you’ve worked as a software developer, chances are you’ve survived one of those corporate cost-cutting crusades where productivity suddenly becomes the magic word for reducing headcount. And guess what management loves to bring up? Yep, you probably guessed it already: the mythical 10x developer. When profits start sinking, you know what a desperate CEO loves to imagine: fewer developers somehow producing ten times more software. Problem solved. And then comes the cherry on top: one of the most misunderstood books in programming history, Frederick P. Brooks Jr.’s The Mythical Man-Month , conveniently twisted into the argument that adding developers only makes projects slower. And if cutting staff means producing more software at a lower cost while boosting profits, what CEO wouldn’t fall in love with that brilliant business strategy? search_index.content: Medium The Study Bitcoin Doesn’t Want You to See | by Chetan Dugar | Coinmonks | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Coinmonks · Coinmonks is a non-profit Crypto Educational Publication. Other Project — https://coincodecap.com/ & Email — gaurav@coincodecap.com Member-only story Blockchain Bitcoin Ethereum Cryptocurrency Crypto The Study Bitcoin Doesn’t Want You to See Chetan Dugar 9 min read · Sep 1, 2026 -- 93 Listen Share Two economists quietly downloaded the entire blockchain and counted who really owns Bitcoin. What they found breaks the one promise the whole thing was built on. Press enter or click to view image in full size “Bitcoin has no kings.” You’ve heard some version of that line a hundred times. No banks. No middlemen. No small room of powerful men deciding what happens to your money while you sleep. Power handed back to regular people. Money for everyone, owned by everyone. It’s a beautiful story. Honestly, it’s one of the most beautiful stories money has ever told about itself. Then, a few years ago, two economists did something almost nobody in this space bothers to do. They didn’t argue about Bitcoin. They didn’t tweet hot takes or go on podcasts. They just… downloaded the whole thing, every transaction since 2009 and counted. What they found doesn’t make it onto any conference slide. Press enter or click to view image in full size The pitch was a world with no kings. Hold that thought. search_index.description: I Let AI Manage My Money for 30 Days. My Bank Account Has Never Looked Better. I was skeptical. Then I saw the numbers. Here’s exactly what I did—and what happened. I’ll be straight with …
search_index.content: Medium I Let AI Manage My Money for 30 Days. My Bank Account Has Never Looked Better. | by Solo | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Solo Personal Finance Finance Money Money Management I Let AI Manage My Money for 30 Days. My Bank Account Has Never Looked Better. Solo 5 min read · Jun 1, 2026 -- 46 Listen Share I was skeptical. Then I saw the numbers. Here’s exactly what I did—and what happened. Press enter or click to view image in full size I’ll be straight with you. I’ve read every “budget better” article on the internet. I’ve downloaded the apps, made the spreadsheets, and bought the journal with the cute expense tracker. Nothing stuck. Then I tried something different. For 30 days, I handed almost every financial decision to AI—budgeting, investing, bill negotiation, spending awareness, and the whole thing. Nearly 49% of global consumers have now used AI to support savings and investment decisions in the past six months. I wanted to find out what the other 51% were missing. Here’s my honest, step-by-step account of what I did, what worked, what didn’t, and how much I actually saved. Week 1: I Found Out Where My Money Was Actually Going The first thing I did was give Claude a full picture of my monthly spending—every category, every rough estimate—and ask it to find the leaks. I expected it to tell me I was spending too much on coffee. It didn’t. It found something worse. I was paying for four overlapping services doing essentially the same thing. Two project management apps. Two cloud storage plans. A VPN I’d forgotten existed. A meditation app I’d used twice in eight months. Total wasted per month: $94. That’s $1,128 a year — gone. Silently. Every single year. The prompt I used: “Here is every subscription and recurring charge I pay monthly: [full list with costs]. Find every overlap, every service with a free alternative, every app I likely underuse based on the category, and rank them by which to cancel first for maximum savings.” What happened next: Cancelled 6 services in one afternoon Found free alternatives for 3 of them Set up family sharing on two others Recovered $94/month starting immediately Week 2: I Stopped Leaving Money on the Table at Tax Time AI identifies tax-saving opportunities in real time — tax-loss harvesting, optimal Roth conversion amounts, charitable giving strategies, and asset location between taxable and tax-advantaged accounts. I’m self-employed part-time. I knew vaguely that I could deduct some things. I had no idea how much I was missing. I described my work setup to Claude—home office, equipment, software, internet, and phone—and asked for every legal deduction I qualified for. The list was longer than I expected. A lot longer. The prompt I used: “I work from home part-time as a [freelancer/creator/consultant]. I use a dedicated home office space of [X sq ft] in a [X sq ft] home. My work-related expenses this year include: [list everything — laptop, software, internet, phone, courses, equipment]. What are every legal tax deduction I can claim, how do I calculate the home office deduction, and what records do I need to keep?” What I discovered: Home office deduction: I’d never claimed it—worth ~$340/year. My entire internet bill is partially deductible Three software subscriptions I was paying personally should be business expenses Professional development courses are fully deductible Estimated annual tax saving: $780 Week 3: I Made My First Investments Without Paying Anyone In 2026, robo-advisors powered by AI allow anyone to start investing with as little as $1. They automatically build a diversified portfolio, rebalance it when the market shifts, and adjust it as your goals change. Credible I’d been “meaning to invest” for two years. The problem wasn’t money. It was paralysis. Every time I researched it, I ended up more confused than when I started. I asked Claude to explain investing to me like I was starting from zero—with my specific income, goals, and timeline. No jargon. No assumptions. Then I asked it to build me a starter plan. The prompt I used: “I am [age] years old. I earn $[amount] per month and can invest $[amount] per month. I’ve never invested before. My goals are [specific goals] in [timeframe]. My risk tolerance is medium. Build me the simplest possible beginner investment plan using index funds and a Roth IRA. Tell me exactly which account to open first, how much to put where, and what to do on day one.” What happened: Opened a Roth IRA the same afternoon Set up a $200/month automatic index fund contribution Finally understood the difference between a Roth IRA and a 401(k) in plain English Stopped being paralyzed by choice The money I invested in Week 3 will be worth dramatically more in 20 years than the money I didn’t invest for the previous two years. That’s the real cost of waiting. Week 4: I Negotiated Two Bills I’d Been Paying Full Price For Most people pay full price for things that are completely negotiable. Some AI-powered services even negotiate your bills — internet, phone, insurance — on your behalf, saving hundreds per year. I used Claude to prepare negotiation scripts for my internet provider and my car insurance renewal. Both calls took under 10 minutes total. The prompt I used: “I’ve been a customer of [provider] for [X years] and currently pay $[amount] per month for [service]. I’ve seen competitor rates as low as $[amount]. Write me a calm, confident 3-minute phone script to negotiate a lower rate or a better deal. Include what to say if they say no the first time, and the exact phrase to use to escalate to the retention department.” Results: Internet bill: dropped from $89/month to $67/month — saving $264/year Car insurance: loyalty discount applied — saving $180/year Total from two 10-minute phone calls: $444/year back in my pocket The Full 30-Day Scorecard Here’s every dollar recovered or redirected in one month: Subscription audit: $94/month saved = $1,128/year Tax

search_index.description: Every person you meet carries a different version of you in their mind Sometimes, we wonder how others perceive us. Perhaps we all want to be seen as nice, kind, or any other words associated with …
search_index.content: Medium Every person you meet carries a different version of you in their mind | by Devina | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Devina Giving you my unprofessional advice (please take everything with a grain of salt) Press enter or click to view image in full size Source: https://pin.it/65PoHONQS Life Self Improvement Psychology Mental Health This Happened To Me Every person you meet carries a different version of you in their mind Devina 3 min read · Jun 1, 2026 -- 575 Listen Share Sometimes, we wonder how others perceive us. Perhaps we all want to be seen as nice, kind, or any other words associated with positive traits. And to be perceived the way we want, we often become extremely careful about how we carry ourselves in society. We measure every interaction. We curate the stories we choose to tell so we won’t be labeled “too much” and we restrain ourselves from doing something silly because we fear being seen as weird. But no matter how carefully you present yourself, there will always be someone who misunderstands you. Someone might think you are shy simply because you are the quietest person in the room. But maybe you are dealing with personal struggles and still choosing to show up, while all you are really doing is being observant. Someone might see you as lonely because you are not married at the age you are “supposed” to be (according to society’s timeline). What they do not know is that you are enjoying your singleness and you are surrounded by good people who make you feel loved. However, there are also people who are inspired by your hard work and touched by your kindness. Then, they tell you how much your existence matters in their lives. People hold different versions of you. Most of the time, their understanding of you is shaped by limited interactions and specific situations. Instead of trying to change people’s opinions about you, use them as an opportunity to understand yourself better. When someone says you are annoying, you can reflect on the situations in which they felt that way and assess yourself. However, that does not mean you should immediately blame yourself and think, “Oh, I shouldn’t speak too much!” Because whatever labels people place on you do not reflect who you are as a person. You are not defined by those perceptions, but rather by how you grow as a human being. The way you change your views or outgrow versions of yourself that no longer align with what you believe. Most importantly, by the way you remain your authentic self, not performing for others just to gain their approval. You don’t have to explain yourself every time someone misunderstands you. Sometimes, it’s useless. Even when you have grown into a different version of yourself, some old school friends might be surprised and say, “Oh, you’re not that shy kid anymore?” They only know the old version of you that still exists in their minds. They forget that people can change. Their opinions of you are not in your control and no matter how hard you try, there is no guarantee that they will change them. If you crave being seen as good and becoming everyone’s favorite, let me tell you this: it’s a myth. No matter how genuine you try to be, there will always be someone who interprets you the wrong way. Even when you believe you are doing what must be done, some people may still see you as the villain. Don’t shrink yourself just to fit into their comfort or to make sure people get the right idea of you. It is such a waste of energy when you have countless responsibilities in life that truly matter. Let people perceive you however they want. Perhaps that is the price you pay for being seen and building human connection. But you can play your part; to live unapologetically and hold firmly to the values you believe in. In short, whatever people think about you, let them live with those thoughts. search_index.description: Join CodeElevation: We’re Seeking Passionate Coding Writers! Are you a coding enthusiast with a knack for writing? Do you love sharing your knowledge and insights about the world of programming …
search_index.content: Medium Join CodeElevation: We’re Seeking Passionate Coding Writers! | by Deo Wetton | CodeElevation | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in CodeElevation · A gathering place for individuals passionate about coding — be it programmers, devs, or engineers. Join CodeElevation: We’re Seeking Passionate Coding Writers! Deo Wetton 3 min read · Feb 23, 2025 -- 159 Listen Share Are you a coding enthusiast with a knack for writing? Do you love sharing your knowledge and insights about the world of programming, development, and engineering? If so, CodeElevation wants you to be a part of our community! Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by Fotis Fotopoulos on Unsplash What We’re Looking For In — Depth Technical Knowledge : We need writers who can break down complex coding concepts, from advanced algorithms to the latest frameworks like React.js or Rust, into understandable and engaging content. Whether it’s about optimizing code for performance or explaining the inner workings of a new programming language feature, your expertise should shine through. Up — to — Date Industry Insights : The tech world moves at a breakneck pace. We’re looking for authors who can keep tabs on the latest trends, such as the rise of artificial intelligence in software development, the implications of serverless computing, or the future of blockchain in coding. Unique and Original Content : We want fresh perspectives. Avoid recycled blog posts or well — trodden topics. Whether it’s a personal experience with a difficult coding project or a new way to approach a common problem, show us something new. Engaging Writing Style : Write in a way that grabs the reader’s attention. Use short paragraphs, code snippets for illustration, and clear headings. Articles should typically be between 1000–2000 words, but we’re open to shorter, more focused pieces as well. Code Examples : Whenever possible, include working code examples. Whether it’s a simple Python script or a complex JavaScript module, code examples help readers better understand the concepts you’re explaining. Examples of Topics We Love Coding Best Practices : Share your top tips for writing clean, maintainable code, no matter the programming language. Case Studies : Walk us through a challenging coding project you’ve worked on, from the initial problem statement to the final solution. New Tools and Technologies : Introduce readers to emerging coding tools like new integrated development environments (IDEs), testing frameworks, or code analysis tools. Coding Interviews : Provide advice on how to ace coding interviews, from preparing algorithms to handling behavioral questions. Why Write for CodeElevation? Build Your Reputation : Gain exposure within the coding community. Your articles will be read by programmers, developers, and engineers from around the world, helping you establish yourself as an authority in the field. Learn and Grow : Engage with other like — minded individuals. Receive feedback on your articles, learn from other writers, and stay at the forefront of the coding world. Share Your Passion : CodeElevation is a place where your love for coding can be shared with a passionate audience. Inspire others, answer questions, and contribute to the growth of the coding community. How to Get Involved Leave a Comment : Drop your username and a brief introduction in the comments section below. Our team of editors will review your submission and get back to you as soon as possible. If your work is a good fit, we’ll work with you to publish your article on CodeElevation! We can’t wait to hear from you and read your amazing coding — related stories! Let’s elevate the coding game together! 🚀 Written by Deo Wetton 2.4K followers · 4.3K following A Full-Stack Developer at a Tech Startup. Follow me for tech insights and problem-solving inspiration! Let's navigate the future of code together!💫 Published in CodeElevation 33K followers · Last published 1 hour ago A gathering place for individuals passionate about coding — be it programmers, devs, or engineers. Medium reserves the right to modify, suspend, or discontinue the Partner Program, or any portion thereof, at any time and without advance notice to you. Medium will not be liable to you or any third party for any such modification, suspension, or termination. By participating in the Partner Program, you agree to these Partner Program Terms, as well as Medium’s Terms of Service , Privacy Policy , Rules , and all other terms and conditions that apply to the Medium website, mobile applications, and any other Medium service or product (collectively, the “Terms”). Please read the Partner Program Terms carefully. If you don’t understand them, or don’t accept any part of them, then you can’t participate in the Partner Program. Your acceptance of Medium’s Partner Program Terms forms a binding agreement between you and Medium and shows your intent to be bound by them. Eligibility To participate in the Partner Program, you must meet the Eligibility Requirements . Medium reserves the right to admit writers to the Partner Program at Medium’s sole discretion. Eligibility requirements are subject to change. Existing Partner Program Participants : If you are a participant in the Partner Program as of August 1, 2024, you will remain in the program. However, to continue to participate in the Partner Program, you’ll need to meet the Eligibility Requirements by December 31, 2024. Medium will use reasonable efforts to contact you before removing you from the Partner Program if you no longer meet the Eligibility Requirements. If you are removed from the Partner Program, your locked stories will be removed from behind the paywall. Ongoing Eligibility for all Partner Program participants : To remain in the Partner Program, you must continue to meet the Eligibility Requirements . In the event that we disable your ability to receive any revenue under the Partner Program and we subsequently determine that you meet the requirements to remain in the Partner Program, we may re-enable your ability to receive revenue under the Partner Program without requiring a reapplication from you for the Partner Program. Earning on Locked Stories User Stories For each locked story associated with your account, you have the opportunity to receive revenue based on various performance factors, including reader engagement. Based on the performance and assessed quality of a story, Medium will pay you a portion of revenues received by Medium from membership fees, as determined by Medium. Medium will send you payment for any revenues above $10 USD accrued as described in the Payment section below. Medium reserves the right to adjust at any time the factors by which story performance and revenue are determined. User Stories & Medium Publications A locked story may be included in a Medium publication. The writer chooses whether to lock a story and will receive the same amount of funds through the Partner Program regardless of whether the story is included in a publication. As with any story, either the writer or the publication owner or editors may choose to remove a locked story from a publication at any time. The above arrangement may be modified on a case-by-case basis, such as for publications operating on Medium that commission or own their content. For any such publication planning to receive proceeds from a story’s performance, this arrangement must be made clear to any writer potentially affected and agreed upon in advance with a given story’s writer. Earning on Editing Activities As a participant in the Partner Program, you will be eligible to apply to participate in Medium’s Editor Partner Program (the “EPP”). Medium reserves the right to admit or reject any applicant to the EPP at Medium’s sole discretion. Eligibility requirements for the EPP are described here and may be changed by Medium at any time without notice. If Medium accepts your application to participate in the EPP, you will be permitted to edit eligible stories submitted to Medium publications of which you are an owner or an editor, in accordance with Medium’s editorial guidelines and policies. For each story you edit, you may earn compensation based on that story’s performance, as described in Medium’s EPP Pay Structure here . Medium retains sole discretion to determine which stories are eligible for editing under the EPP. Medium reserves the right to modify, suspend, or discontinue the EPP, or any portion thereof, at any time and without advance notice to you. Note to Writers Stories submitted to Medium may be edited by an editor participating in EPP. EPP editors may receive compensation from Medium based on the performance of stories they edit. search_index.content: Medium About Medium About Medium Sitemap Sign in Sign up Everyone has a story to tell Medium is a home for human stories and ideas. Here, anyone can share knowledge and wisdom with the world—without having to build a mailing list or a following first. The internet is noisy and chaotic; Medium is quiet yet full of insight. It’s simple, beautiful, collaborative, and helps you find the right readers for whatever you have to say. Ultimately, our goal is to deepen our collective understanding of the world through the power of writing. We believe that what you read and write matters. Words can divide or empower us, inspire or discourage us. In a world where the most sensational and surface-level stories often win, we’re building a system that rewards depth, nuance, and time well spent. A space for thoughtful conversation more than drive-by takes, and substance over packaging. Over 100 million people connect and share their wisdom on Medium every month. They’re software developers, amateur novelists, product designers, CEOs, and anyone burning with a story they need to get out into the world. They write about what they’re working on, what’s keeping them up at night, what they’ve lived through, and what they’ve learned that the rest of us might want to know too. Instead of selling ads or selling your data, we’re supported by a growing community of over a million Medium members who believe in our mission. If you’re new here, start reading . Dive deeper into whatever matters to you. Find a post that helps you learn something new, or reconsider something familiar—and then write your story . search_index.description: How I Accidentally Started Selling Digital Products (And Almost Quit After the First One) I didn’t plan any of this. Three years ago I was just trying to organize my own finances. Nothing fancy. A …
search_index.content: Medium How I Accidentally Started Selling Digital Products (And Almost Quit After the First One) | by Stave | Sep, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Passive Income Small Business Productivity Ecommerce How I Accidentally Started Selling Digital Products (And Almost Quit After the First One) Stave 3 min read · Sep 23, 2026 -- 3 Listen Share I didn’t plan any of this. Three years ago I was just trying to organize my own finances. Nothing fancy. A simple budget tracker in Notion because I was tired of forgetting where my money went every month. A friend saw it over my shoulder and asked if I’d sell it to her. I said sure, $5 , why not. That was the whole plan. There was no plan. I cleaned it up a little, made the categories make sense to someone who wasn’t me, and put it up for $19 because a random blog post said templates under $20 sell better. I still don’t know if that’s true. I just believed it because it was Tuesday and I needed a number. The first sale came four days later. I refreshed my email like it owed me something. $19. Minus whatever the platform takes. Somewhere around $16 landed in my account, and I remember being disproportionately excited about sixteen dollars. Then nothing happened for almost three weeks. I checked constantly. I convinced myself the product was bad, the price was wrong, nobody actually wanted this, and I should just take it down before it embarrassed me further. I didn’t take it down. Mostly because I forgot which app the delete button was even in. Sale two came in week four. Then two more the week after that. I still wasn’t posting about it anywhere, which in hindsight explains most of the silence. That accidental template is the same one from my last post here, still one of seven things I sell now, still bringing in a few hundred dollars most months without me touching the file itself. Here’s roughly how the other six happened, since none of them were planned either. A PDF guide, because I kept answering the same freelance pricing question in DMs and got tired of retyping it. A template pack, made in one weekend because I was avoiding a different, harder project. A calculator, built for myself first, same as the very first one. A printable, priced low on purpose just to see if volume alone could work. It did. A swipe file, pulled straight from my own sent folder. A photo pack I almost didn’t finish, sitting in a folder for two months before I uploaded it out of guilt more than confidence. None of them started as a business idea. They started as me solving something annoying for myself, then noticing someone else had the same annoying problem. The part nobody tells you is that making the thing is maybe twenty percent of it. The rest is just showing up around it, again and again, long after it stops feeling new. I was bad at that part for the first year. Genuinely bad. I’d post once, wait, get discouraged by silence, and go quiet for two weeks. That’s honestly the only thing that’s really changed since then. Not the products and not some big strategy shift. Just actually staying visible consistently, which used to eat my whole week until I started running that part through Nuno Ai instead of doing it by hand every night. Press enter or click to view image in full size that’s how this AI works ( getnuno.com ) I didn’t mean to write this much. I sat down to tell the short version of how the first template happened and ended up telling you about all seven. Great thanks for your time. hope u learned something… If you’ve got something sitting in a folder right now that you built for yourself and never sold, what’s actually stopping you from putting a price on it this week? search_index.content: Medium The Unsexy Way to Make Money With Nuno AI Mimic | by Stave | Oct, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Mimic AI Video Unsexy Recreation The Unsexy Way to Make Money With Nuno AI Mimic Stave 5 min read · Oct 18, 2026 -- Listen Share I’m Testing It Right Now Nuno Mimic recreation ss Let me start with the part most posts about making money online skip. I haven’t earned a dollar from this yet. What I have is a plan, some math I checked twice, and a list of ways it could fall apart. I’m writing it all down before I start, because the last few times I tested something the real numbers came in smaller than my hopes, and I’d rather be honest from the first page than the last one. What Mimic actually does Here’s Nuno AI Mimic in the plainest words I have. You pick any character, and you see that character in the exact video. Same video, different cast. I keep it that simple on purpose. Press enter or click to view image in full size The simplest version of a tool is the one you can explain to a friend in one breath, and if you can’t explain it that fast, you can’t sell it that fast either. It matters because every few weeks some video format takes over the feed, and every small business owner I know says the same thing. We should do that. Then they don’t, because making their own version means finding someone to film, someone to edit, and a week they don’t have. By the time it’s done, the trend has moved on. Why someone would pay for it This is the unsexy part, and it’s the part I like. I’m not talking about going viral. I’m talking about a bakery, a dentist, a plumber, a candle shop. People who are busy running something real and who’d love a funny, current-looking post on their page without lifting a finger. Press enter or click to view image in full size featured clips on Nuno Mimic A person who can take a format that’s already working and hand back a finished post, with the business’s own mascot or character in it, a caption written, and the whole thing scheduled, is selling something very plain. A Tuesday post that exists. That’s a boring product, and boring is the thing I’ve learned to trust. Most of what I sell is boring. The plan and the math The plan is small. I pick three local businesses I already know, and I offer each one a month of four recast posts, with captions and scheduling included. I’m starting at $250 a month. That’s an example I picked because it’s easy to defend, not a market rate anyone should copy, and the first thing I’ll learn is whether it’s too high or too low. Three clients at $250 is $750 a month. Now the part that decides whether it’s any good. I’m guessing that four posts for one client takes me about two and a half hours a month, counting the brief, the character, the caption, and the scheduling. I don’t know that yet. If the guess is right, three clients is 7.5 hours for $750, which works out to about $100 an hour. If it’s really four hours per client, that’s 12 hours and about $62.50 an hour. Same plan, very different job. Measuring the real number in month one matters more than anything else on this list. Two more lines on the math. Subtract whatever the tool costs per month, and check Nuno’s current pricing instead of trusting my memory of it. If one client’s fee doesn’t cover that comfortably, the price is wrong. And expect people to leave. If I lose one client in five each month, three clients becomes closer to two and a half on average, so I plan around two. Two clients is $500. That isn’t life-changing money. It’s also about the size of the first thing that worked for me every time, which is why I’m not embarrassed by it. The ceiling here isn’t the tool. It’s finding clients. Past three, every extra business means more outreach before it means more production, so that’s where I expect to be slow. Mimic makes the video. Nuno handles the rest of the work around it: writing the caption in a business’s voice once it has learned the brand from a link, planning the week, and posting or scheduling to the accounts, so three clients don’t turn into three sets of tabs and three nights of copy and paste. Nuno also has an affiliate program for people who recommend it. I’m not building anything around that yet, and I’ll read the current terms before I say a word about them. What could go wrong A few things, and I’d rather list them now. Rights come first. A client has to own or be licensed to use any character that appears in a post, and I’d want that in writing. Famous characters stay off business accounts, full stop. The original video matters too. Check that the person who made it is fine with it being reused, credit them where that’s the right call, and follow each platform’s own rules on remixes. This is general guidance, not legal advice. Next, results. A recast is a post. It isn’t a promise of views, and I’m not going to tell any business it will go viral. I’d sell the finished work, not the outcome. Third, fit. Some audiences will love a playful post and some will wonder why their accountant is acting strange. I’d start with businesses whose customers already like a joke. Last, time. If the two and a half hours is really five, the whole thing stops being worth it at $250, and I’d rather find that out in week two than month six. What I’m doing this week I’m messaging three businesses I already buy from and offering each of them one free recast post, no strings, to see if they’d want a month. I’m writing down how long each one takes, what they say, and whether the post does anything at all. Then I’ll come back with the real numbers, including the ones I won’t enjoy. If it flops, that’s the post I’ll write instead. Press enter or click to view image in full size Nuno Mimic: https://getnuno.com/mimic Thanks for reading this one. In the winter it’s not a problem for them to fall asleep, because it gets dark early, but summer makes it… - Noor Write’s - Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Noor Write’s Just me & my writing ✍️ Member-only story Books History Medium Partner Program Writing Creativity Noor Write’s Nov 7, 2026 -- 3 Listen Share Bed In Summer By Robert Louis Stevenson FAMOUS POEM Most children have an early bedtime. In the winter it’s not a problem for them to fall asleep, because it gets dark early, but summer makes it difficult. With more daylight, children long to be able to play until the sun dips far below the horizon. in Famous Children Poems In Winter I get up at night And dress by yellow candle light. In Summer, quite the other way, I have to go to bed by day. I have to go to bed and see The birds still hopping on the tree, Or hear the grown-up people’s feet Still going past me in the street. And does it not seem hard to you, When all the sky is clear and blue, And I should like so much to play, To have to go to bed by day? search_index.description: A Lesson from a Wise Old Man in Africa Years ago, I sat under a tree in a small village in Africa, talking with an old man who had spent his life as a village elder – respected, loved, and …
search_index.content: Medium A Lesson from a Wise Old Man in Africa | by Noor Write’s | Nov, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Noor Write’s Just me & my writing ✍️ Member-only story Books Culture History Medium Partner Program Personal Growth A Lesson from a Wise Old Man in Africa Noor Write’s 2 min read · Nov 8, 2026 -- 4 Listen Share Years ago, I sat under a tree in a small village in Africa, talking with an old man who had spent his life as a village elder – respected, loved, and constantly surrounded by people. At one point, I asked him, “How did you become the person everyone comes to for advice, help, even food when times are tough?” He smiled, leaned in, and said something I’ll never forget: “If you want to eat well for a week, grow crops. If you want to eat well for a season, raise animals. But if you want to eat well for life, grow people.” He wasn’t talking about clients, marketing, or business – but the lesson stuck. Because in business, the ones who grow people, through relationships, care, and community… are the ones who never run out of referrals, word of mouth, or clients. Here’s what I took from that conversation and it changed everything: Grow Relationships, Not Just a List People refer people they trust. That trust is earned through real conversations, not transactions. 2. Stay Front of Mind, Like the Village Drummer The drummer in the village plays daily – not because people forget the rhythm, but because consistency brings people together. Your network needs to hear your drum often. How to maximise your Medium audience | by Nassos Michas | Mac O’Clock | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Mastodon Mac O’Clock · The best stories for Apple owners and enthusiasts Member-only story Apple Medium Creative Writing Writing Publication Guidelines Booost! How to maximise your Medium audience Nassos Michas 5 min read · May 31, 2023 -- 8 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by Brian McGowan on Unsplash Have you ever written a story just to receive an email from Medium a couple of days later telling you that “your story was boosted”? And did your story-statistics looked like this before and after that boost? A story being accepted for Boost (image by author) Well done! You have been… booosted! Oh, you do not know what Boost is? Keep reading, we have gathered all the juicy details we know about Boost next. What is Boost? Boost is a program introduced by Medium on February 2023. Boost tries to identify the best stories in Medium and expose them to a wider audience. There is no guarantee as to how much such exposure will affect the number of your readers, however practice shows you gain an initial boost of a few hundreds to a few thousands of additional readers. How long Boost lasts for? Boost does not last for very long; usually, it lasts for just a few days. And that is good. The essence of Boost is not to provide you additional readership in perpetuity, but to bring to the surface stories, or writers, that are of exceptional quality but otherwise might have gone relatively unnoticed. search_index.content: Medium 30-Day Beginner Workout Plan at Home: The Simple Routine Most Beginners Get Wrong | by We Care | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in We Care Here to help Mental Health Wellness Fitness Health We Care 2 min read · Aug 25, 2026 -- Listen Share 30-Day Beginner Workout Plan at Home: The Simple Routine Most Beginners Get Wrong Press enter or click to view image in full size Starting your fitness journey doesn't have to mean spending hours in the gym. But there's one mistake many beginners make... They try to do too much, too soon. You don't need 100 push-ups, a complicated gym routine, or expensive equipment to start making progress. You need a simple system you can actually stick to. The Problem With Most Beginner Workout Plans Search for a beginner workout plan online and you'll find hundreds of different routines. The problem? Most people don't know: Which exercises to start with How many days they should train When they should rest How to progress What to do when motivation disappears And that's where many beginners give up. What If You Only Had 7 Days? Imagine having a simple schedule telling you exactly what to focus on each day. No guessing. No complicated equipment. No spending hours trying to figure out what to do next. The first few days are designed to help you get moving. Then something changes... Day 4 is where many beginners make a mistake. Instead of simply pushing harder, you need to understand how to use recovery and progression properly. And that's just one part of the system. The Secret Isn't Working Harder The goal isn't to destroy yourself during every workout. The goal is to build a routine you can repeat. Once you understand how to structure your workouts, recovery, and progression, your fitness journey becomes much easier to manage. Want the complete plan? I've put together a 30-Day Workout Plan with a structured approach to help you stop guessing and start following a consistent routine. 👉 Get the complete 30-Day Workout Plan on Gumroad https://shorturl.at/36N2B Your first week doesn't need to be perfect. It just needs to be the week you finally start. Disclaimer: This article is for general educational purposes and isn't medical advice. search_index.content: Why every hospital needs a modern tool to manage its surgical dictionary | IMO Health Skip to content Why every hospital needs a modern tool to manage its surgical dictionary Running a surgical department costs millions of dollars per year. Advanced tools can boost financial performance, operational efficiency, and clinical care. Published September 9, 2025 Written by Linda Casey, MS, MPH Senior Product Manager, IMO Core Periop Precision and efficiency are essential in the surgical environment. Every procedure scheduled, documented, and billed depends on the accuracy of a hospital’s surgical dictionary . Yet many organizations still rely on outdated, incomplete, or inconsistent terminology, introducing risk, inefficiency, and revenue loss into critical workflows. A smart, centralized tool for surgical dictionary management is a necessity. Here’s why: 1. The surgical dictionary: A clinical and financial anchor A surgical dictionary is the foundation of perioperative operations. It contains: Standardized names of procedures Associated CPT® and HCPCS codes Inpatient-only (IPO) and Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) covered and excluded flags Patient-friendly descriptors This dictionary is used across multiple workflows, including: Surgery scheduling : Ensures the correct procedure is selected and routed to the appropriate surgical team and location. Documentation : Supports accurate clinical records and aligns with coding standards. Pre-authorizations : Helps verify coverage and avoid delays in care. Compliance and billing : Reduces the risk of coding errors and claim denials. When surgical dictionaries are well-managed, the impact is measurable. One organization saw a 57% reduction in IPO denials and reclaimed $3 million in revenue after implementing IMO Health’s perioperative solution. These aren’t just operational wins – they’re strategic outcomes that directly affect patient care and financial performance. 2. Full visibility: Why seeing the entire dictionary matters Many hospitals struggle to manage their surgical dictionaries because they lack a complete view of the content. Without full visibility, it becomes difficult to identify outdated terms, duplications, or inconsistencies. A modern tool addresses this challenge by providing comprehensive access to all dictionary entries in one place , while also enabling cross-departmental alignment so clinical, IT, and revenue cycle teams can collaborate on updates. This visibility empowers hospitals to clean up legacy content, standardize terminology, and ensure that every term in the dictionary is appropriate for accurately scheduling surgeries. 3. Service line filtering: Empowering clinical review Surgical dictionaries often contain thousands of procedures, making it overwhelming for clinical teams to focus on those relevant to their specialty. Service line filtering helps by allowing users to display terms by specialty, such as orthopedics, cardiology, or general surgery. This approach streamlines clinical validation by narrowing the scope of review, while also encouraging ownership by enabling service line leaders to take responsibility for their content. As a result, clinicians can more easily engage in the review process, ensuring that the dictionary reflects current procedures, IPO and ASC flags, and associated CPT and HCPCS codes. 4. Avoiding claim denials: IPO and ASC Code visibility Claim denials are a major source of lost revenue – and many are preventable. A built-in dictionary management tool provides visibility into IPO and ASC coverage rules. With this functionality, hospitals can: Flag IPO procedures to avoid scheduling in outpatient settings Identify ASC-covered or excluded codes to ensure compliance with payer rules Facilitate preauthorization workflows by providing pertinent site-of-care information during the scheduling process These capabilities help prevent total-loss denials, reduce rework, and protect revenue integrity across the surgical service line. 5. Metadata that matters: Enhancing usability and communication A surgical dictionary isn’t just a resource for coders – it is used by schedulers, clinicians, and administrative staff across the organization. That’s why metadata plays such a vital role. In-workflow tools enhance usability by incorporating patient-friendly terms that improve communication with patients and families, synonyms and aliases that reflect how procedures are commonly referred to in practice, and internal identifiers that support mapping across systems and workflows. Together, these elements improve searchability, reduce ambiguity, and ensure that everyone –from the OR to the front desk – speaks the same language. A strategic asset, not just a dictionary A surgical dictionary is not just a technical tool; it plays a crucial role in all areas of perioperative operations. It becomes a powerful enabler of clinical excellence, operational efficiency, and financial performance when managed properly. Hospitals that invest in a surgical dictionary management solution gain: Operational efficiency : By streamlining scheduling, documentation, and reviewing workflows, hospitals reduce administrative burden and eliminate redundant manual processes. Teams can work faster and with greater confidence, knowing that the terms they’re using are accurate and current. Clinical accuracy : With service line filtering and clinician-friendly metadata, clinical teams can validate and maintain the dictionary in a way that reflects real-world practice. This ensures that surgical terms are not only technically correct but clinically meaningful. Revenue protection and growth : Built-in visibility into IPO and ASC coverage rules helps prevent costly claim denials. Accurate coding and preauthorization support lead to faster reimbursements and fewer revenue leaks. We did the math to see just how much those extra minutes cost. Published March 9, 2022 Written by IMO Health Staff Time is money. When it comes to the operating room, the old adage couldn’t be more spot on. Even five wasted minutes during a single case can cost a health system hundreds – if not thousands – of dollars. Factor in the number of cases performed each day, week, or year, and the numbers can be truly shocking. What’s more, an OR sitting empty – if, for example, a case finished early – has a different financial impact than one that runs over its allotted time block. It’s a lot to keep track of, and it’s not necessarily easy to see just how much money case duration inaccuracies leave on the proverbial (OR) table. So we did some math to help visualize how scheduling just one procedure using a generic surgical term – craniotomy – can lighten a health system’s ledger. search_index.title: 2027 OPPS and ASC proposed rule: 6 changes that could reshape outpatient care | IMO Health
search_index.description: Payment, reimbursement, authorization, and site-of-care requirements are shifting. Here’s what health systems should know for 2027 and beyond.
search_index.content: 2027 OPPS and ASC proposed rule: 6 changes that could reshape outpatient care | IMO Health Skip to content 2027 OPPS and ASC proposed rule: 6 changes that could reshape outpatient care Payment, reimbursement, authorization, and site-of-care requirements are shifting. Here’s what health systems should know for 2027 and beyond. Published October 28, 2026 Written by Shelly L. Jude, RHIA, RHIT, HIT Global Clinical Services Director The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) has proposed updates to the Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) and Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) Payment System for calendar year 2027. The proposals would affect approximately 3,500 hospitals and 6,400 ASCs and include changes to payment rates, site-of-service policies , drug reimbursement, prior authorization , and quality reporting. As outpatient care evolves, health systems are navigating increasingly complex requirements around where procedures are performed, how they are reimbursed, and what is required to support them. Below, we outline six key changes health systems should prepare for. 1. 2027 OPPS and ASC payment update CMS is proposing a 2.4% payment-rate increase for hospitals that meet applicable quality reporting requirements. Qualifying ASCs would receive the same update. The proposal is based on a projected 3.2% hospital market basket increase, reduced by a 0.8 percentage-point productivity adjustment. 2. Continued phaseout of the inpatient-only list CMS is continuing its three-year phaseout of the Inpatient Only (IPO) list . For 2027, the agency is proposing to remove 638 additional services across clinical families including digestive, endocrine, respiratory, urinary, integumentary, maternity and delivery, and others. If finalized, the change would allow Medicare to pay for these services in the hospital outpatient setting when clinically appropriate, giving physicians greater flexibility in choosing the right site of care. The proposal follows the removal of 285 codes finalized for 2026, marking the first year of the phase-out. As more procedures become eligible for outpatient care, health systems need to keep scheduling, authorization, and reimbursement workflows aligned with changing site-of-care policies. 3. Expansion of site-neutral payments CMS is proposing to expand site-neutral payment policies by paying a Physician Fee Schedule-equivalent rate for certain imaging services without contrast at excepted off-campus provider-based departments. Rural Sole Community Hospitals would be exempt. CMS estimates the change would reduce Medicare Part B expenditures by approximately $260 million in the first year. Building on earlier policies affecting clinic visits and drug-administration services, the proposal reflects CMS’s continued efforts to reduce payment differences based on where care is delivered. 4. Changes to 340B drug reimbursement The proposed rule also includes significant changes for hospitals participating in the 340B Drug Pricing Program . Based on a 2026 hospital drug acquisition cost survey, CMS proposes reimbursing 340B-acquired drugs at Average Sales Price (ASP) minus 33.4% . The agency estimates this would reduce Original Medicare drug payments by $4.55 billion and beneficiary payments by $1.15 billion in the first year. To maintain budget neutrality, CMS proposes a corresponding increase in OPPS payments for non-drug services. CMS also proposes accelerating the existing 340B remedy offset by increasing the reduction to the OPPS conversion factor for affected non-drug services from 0.5% to 3% beginning in 2027. The agency estimates this would achieve the targeted $7.8 billion reduction by 2029. Together, these proposals could significantly affect outpatient reimbursement for participating hospitals. 5. Expansion of prior authorization requirements CMS proposes adding eight botulinum toxin injection codes to its prior authorization requirements for hospital outpatient departments, citing utilization increases and program-integrity concerns. For providers, the proposal underscores the importance of identifying applicable authorization requirements before performing procedures to help reduce avoidable delays and reimbursement risk. 6. Quality reporting changes for hospitals and ASCs CMS is proposing updates to both the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting (OQR) and ASC Quality Reporting (ASCQR) programs . One change would remove the Appropriate Follow-Up Interval for Normal Colonoscopy in Average Risk Patients measure from both programs beginning with the CY 2027 reporting period for the CY 2029 payment determination. CMS notes that another existing colonoscopy measure is more closely tied to clinical outcomes. Quality reporting also carries financial implications. Hospitals and eligible ASCs that fail to meet applicable reporting requirements may receive a two-percentage-point reduction to their annual payment-rate update. What these changes mean for health systems Taken together, the proposed policies reinforce a common challenge: health systems must keep pace with evolving requirements for where procedures are performed, authorized, and reimbursed. Accurate surgical data is critical to navigating these changes. That content supports appropriate site-of-care decisions, consistent workflows, and reimbursement accuracy. IMO Health helps health systems navigate this complexity through standardized surgical terminology and maintained procedural content. Its perioperative offering includes IPO-list and ASC-inclusive code identification to support scheduling, prior authorization, and revenue tracking as CMS policies evolve. Gearing up for 2027? Make OPPS and ASC readiness part of the plan. Talk with an IMO Health expert about how standardized procedural data can help. search_index.content: CPT codes 101: A quick guide to Current Procedural Terminology Skip to content CPT codes 101: A quick guide to Current Procedural Terminology Explore our blog for answers to frequently asked questions about CPT® codes, including their use, maintenance, and categories. Published January 7, 2025 Written by Megan Hillgard Sr. Marketing Campaign Manager Table of Contents Continue reading for answers to commonly asked questions around CPT codes. Use the table of contents to the left to jump ahead to any question. What is Current Procedural Terminology? CPT stands for Current Procedural Terminology. It is a set of codes created by the American Medical Association (AMA®) to standardize how medical procedures are recorded in a medical chart. Why are CPT codes used? CPT codes are one of the primary ways that both public and private medical providers and healthcare institutions can report the services they have provided to patients to the government and insurance companies for reimbursement purposes. CPT codes are part of the national coding system under the Health Information Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). CASE STUDY SPOTLIGHT As Piedmont Healthcare expanded its footprint, they found that their new locations didn’t always speak the same language when it came to surgical and procedure codes. In fact, procedure terms were not mapped to Current Procedural Terminology (CPT®) codes that help ensure accurate scheduling and prior authorization approval. Learn how integrating IMO Health’s surgical terminology and scheduling solution into their EHR allowed them to have each term accurately mapped to the corresponding CPT codes – strengthening communication and accuracy throughout the organization. Read case study How are CPT codes maintained? CPT codes are maintained by the CPT Editorial Board, a part of the AMA, and are updated once a year. The new codes are released annually in November, and go into effect on the following January 1. The editorial board meets three times a year to review applications for new codes. What do CPT codes look like? CPT codes are five characters long and are usually numeric, although some may be alphanumeric depending on what category they fall into. What are the “categories” you mentioned? The CPT manual is divided into three categories, each with distinct purposes outlined below: Category I Used to report the devices and drugs used during a procedure Used to report the procedure itself to the billing department Contains the billable codes needed for reimbursement Category II Designed for reporting performance measures Used to provide data to regulatory agencies Does not contain billing codes Primarily thought of as “quality of care” codes Category III Codes for documenting new procedures, clinical trials and emerging technologies Must be either added to Category I or deleted within five years of being added What are E/M codes and why are they relevant? E/M codes, or Evaluation and Management codes , are part of the CPT system. They are used by healthcare providers to bill for services like office visits, hospital stays, and emergency room care, where they evaluate a patient’s condition and plan treatment. These codes help ensure consistent billing by classifying services based on factors such as the complexity of care or the time spent with the patient. Recent CPT updates focus more on medical decision-making and time, making it easier for providers to choose the correct code without excessive documentation. What is HCPCS and why is it relevant? Another important code set to pair with CPT is the Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System (HCPCS). By presenting HCPCS codes alongside standard CPT codes in EHR scheduling workflows , clinicians and schedulers easily capture increased detail for each procedure. Search PubMed How do I search PubMed? I retrieved too many citations. How can I focus my search? I retrieved too few citations. How can I expand my search? Find a specific citation Searching by author Searching by journal Searching by date Filters Searching for a phrase Wildcards and truncation Combining search terms with Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT) Using search field tags Proximity searching How do I search PubMed? Identify the key concepts for your search. Enter the terms (or key concepts) in the search box. Press the Enter key or click Search. For many searches, it is not necessary to use special tags or syntax. PubMed uses multiple tools to help you find relevant results: Best Match sort order uses a state-of-the-art machine learning algorithm to place the most relevant citations at the top of your results. An autocomplete feature displays suggestions as you type your search terms. This feature is based on PubMed query log analysis described in " Finding Query Suggestions for PubMed ." A spell checking feature suggests alternative spellings for search terms that may include misspellings. A citation sensor displays suggested results for searches that include terms characteristic of citation searching, e.g., author names, journal titles, publication dates, and article titles. I retrieved too many citations. How can I focus my search? To limit the number of search results: Replace general search terms with more specific ones (e.g., low back pain instead of back pain). Include additional terms in your query. Use the sidebar filters to restrict results by publication date, full text availability, article type, and more. I retrieved too few citations. How can I expand my search? On the abstract page for a citation, see the Similar Articles section for a pre-calculated set of additional PubMed citations closely related to that article. Remove extraneous or specific terms from the search box. Try using alternative terms to describe the concepts you are searching. Find a specific citation Paste the article title into the search box, or enter citation details such as the author, journal name and the year the article was published in the search box and the PubMed citation sensor will automatically analyze your query for citation information to return the correct citation. The citation sensor incorporates a fuzzy matching algorithm and will retrieve the best match even if a search includes an incorrect term. You do not need to use field tags or Boolean operators. Searching by author Enter the author’s last name and initials without punctuation in the search box, and click Search. If you only know the author’s last name, use the author search field tag [au], e.g., brody[au]. Names entered using either the lastname+initials format (e.g., smith ja) or the full name format (john a smith) and no search tag are searched as authors as well as collaborators, if they exist in PubMed. Enter a full author name in natural or inverted order, e.g., julia s wong or wong julia s. Prior to 2002, full author names were not included on PubMed citations, so full author name searches will only retrieve citations from 2002 forward, when the full author name was published in the article. A comma following the last name for searching is optional. For some names, however, it is necessary to distinguish which name is the last name by using the comma following the last name, e.g., james, ryan. Omit periods after initials and put all suffixes at the end, e.g., vollmer charles jr Initials and suffixes are not required. If you include a middle initial or suffix, you will only retrieve citations for articles that were published using the middle initial or suffix. More information about author searching: To search by author using the search builder, click Advanced search and then select Author from the All Fields menu. The author search box includes an autocomplete feature. You may click an author link on the abstract display to execute a search for the author in PubMe

search_index.content: Journal Selection for MEDLINE Skip to main content Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock A locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. Menu Journal Selection for MEDLINE The National Library of Medicine (NLM) decides whether the scientific and editorial character and quality of a journal merit its inclusion in MEDLINE. In making this decision, NLM considers scientific policy set by the NLM Board of Regents , the suitability of the journal for the NLM Collection (according to the criteria in the Collection Development Guidelines ), as well as the recommendations of external, expert consultants. At least two consultants, usually one scientist (i.e., doctoral-level researchers or physicians) and one medical librarian review each journal. The consultants generally review articles from the last two years of journal content and evaluate them primarily based on scientific and editorial quality. Their recommendations are taken into consideration by NLM in reaching a final decision on selecting a title for inclusion in MEDLINE. MEDLINE’s Scientific Quality Review is a rigorous, multi-step process in which many factors are assessed. NLM views each journal comprehensively, rather than basing a decision on a defined list of criteria. Each title is reviewed by multiple individuals both internal and external to NLM, and final decisions are based on input from all these sources. A description of possible considerations during the Scientific Quality Review is given below. For an overview of the MEDLINE pre-application requirements as well as a step-by-step breakdown of the MEDLINE application and review process, please see MEDLINE Application and Evaluation Process . Scientific and Editorial Quality Assessment The scientific and editorial quality assessment for MEDLINE focuses on 5 critical elements, listed in the table below. Examples of the types of questions the reviewers may consider for each element are also provided. Critical Element Possible Considerations Scope and Coverage Are the journal’s aims and scope clearly stated? How does the scope of the journal contribute to the field of biomedicine? Does the authorship, editorial board makeup, and content accurately reflect the journal’s scope? (E.g., is authorship international or local/regional? What article types are published in the journal and on what topics?) Does the journal cover an area of research and/or geographic location that is relatively under-represented in the scientific literature? Editorial Policies and Processes Is the peer review process explicit and sufficiently detailed, including information on the type of peer review and the number of reviewers typically assigned to a manuscript? Does the journal have a policy for the review of articles authored by editors and editorial board members (if applicable)? Are the journal’s ethical policies findable, clearly stated, and consistent with current best practices? Are statements regarding approval from an ethics committee and/or regulatory body (animal or human subjects), and informed consent present in all relevant articles? Do authors consistently disclose conflicts of interest and funding sources? Are commercial sponsorships clearly addressed (i.e., do not raise questions about the objectivity of published content)? Are full names, affiliations, and credentials provided for the journal’s editors/editorial board? Do members of the editorial board have appropriate credentials and subject matter expertise? Is the role of editors, editorial board members, and other editorial staff clear? Is there sufficient variation in the editorial board and the authorship of articles? Do journal policies support transparency, reproducibility, open science, and data sharing? Scientific Rigor ¹ /Methodological Rigor ² Does the abstract provide a complete and accurate description of the content of the article? Are study aims clearly stated and logical? Is the rationale/justification for conducting the study clear? Are the methods described in sufficient detail so that the experiment could be reproduced? Are the contents reported in a manner that is consistent with reporting guidelines for the article/study type? Is the study design robust and appropriate to the stated aim? Are the conclusions drawn supported by the data? Is the discussion section critical and comprehensive? Are the references appropriate in number and up-to-date? Are statements supported appropriately by citations? Production and Administration Does the journal keep to its stated publication schedule? Does the publication frequency and volume demonstrate long-term sustainability? Are figures and tables well-constructed and of sufficiently high resolution (i.e., not blurry)? Are figures and tables well-annotated and easy to read and interpret? Is the writing clear, concise, and logical? Does the writing impede scientific meaning or cause confusion? Are authors listed with affiliations and correspondence information? Do articles of the same type (i.e., original research) follow a consistent structure, outlined in the instructions for authors? Do original research articles, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses have structured abstracts? Are there indicators of sufficient editorial attention, as evidenced by the elimination of editorial errors (e.g., incorrectly numbered sections, mislabeled tables/figures)? Is the website functional and easy to use/navigate? Can individual articles be downloaded? In what format(s) is journal content available (e.g., PDF, HTML)? Impact What is the overall significance ³ of the journal? Does the journal critically synthesize and organize knowledge in its field? Footnotes: ¹NLM uses the definition of scientific rigor provided by the NIH Office of

Search PMC Full-Text Archive Search in PMC Journal List User Guide Accessing PMC Article Datasets Using Amazon Web Services As part of our Cloud Service , PMC makes the datasets described below freely accessible on Amazon Web Services (AWS), without charge, through either an HTTPS or S3 URL, and without any log-in requirement for retrieval. The National Library of Medicine works with the AWS Open Data Sponsorship Program to provide this access. Read on to learn why and how you may access these datasets from our AWS Cloud Service. August 26, 2026: PMC's Article Dataset Distribution Service Changes Are Complete Changes to PMC's Article Dataset Distribution Service, first announced in February , are now complete. All legacy PMC Article Dataset files on the FTP and Cloud Services were removed the week of August 24, 2026. For complete details about this transition, please see the NCBI Insights blog post and our documentation on Accessing PMC Article Datasets Using Amazon Web Services Description and Location of PMC Article Datasets on AWS Resource type S3 Bucket, world-readable Amazon Resource Name (ARN) arn:aws:s3:::pmc-oa-opendata AWS Regions us-east-1 AWS Regions us-east-1 Add --no-sign-request to any AWS CLI command to access the bucket anonymously. The README.txt file in the S3 bucket is kept up to date with technical information such as: Structure of the Datasets Inventory Versioning and Update Frequency S3 Bucket Schematic Overview AWS CLI Data Access Using an eSearch-S3 Pipeline FAQs Q: How does versioning work and which version should I use? A: Most articles in the PMC Article Datasets have only one version, version 1. When multiple versions do exist, it is for one of two reasons: The journal or preprint server uses versions. If the journal or preprint server versions their articles, PMC maintains those versions. PMC holds both an author manuscript and a final published version. You can identify author manuscripts using the is_manuscript property in the article's JSON metadata ojbect (set to "yes"). See Author Manuscripts in PMC for more information. The version number reflects the sequence in which PMC processed the deposited versions. PMC does not create a new version when changes are made to an article's content or metadata. When an article is updated, the LastModifiedDate in the inventory and the MD5 values in the JSON metadata object will reflect the update, but no new version prefix is created. See About the Content in PMC for an overview of the types of content in PMC. A higher version number does not mean the version is more recent or should be preferred over a lower-numbered version, except for case 1 above. Version numbers are assigned sequentially as PMC processes file sets, but the version number alone does not indicate whether a version is the author manuscript or is the final published version. It does not indicate which version is preferred for a given use case. To determine what a given version is, inspect its JSON metadata object, which indicates whether it is an author manuscript (is_manuscript). The inventory documentation in the README.txt file describes the fields available in the JSON metadata objects. If a version is removed from the S3 bucket, its prefix and all associated files are deleted from the bucket with no explicit notification. Inventory reconciliation is the only supported way to detect removals. See Accessing the Inventory in the README.txt file for details on working with inventory snapshots. Q: Why is there a version 2 but no version 1 in the dataset? A: In some cases you may find that a prefix such as PMC12805672.2 exists in the bucket while PMC12805672.1 does not. This commonly occurs when version 1 does not have an appropriate license and therefore is not part of the PMC Article Datasets. Do not assume that a version 1 always exists for every PMCID in the S3 bucket. Q: How current is the inventory? Will articles added or updated today appear in it? A: The S3 Inventory is generated once per day. The inventory always lags the current state of the bucket — articles added, updated, or removed since the most recent snapshot was generated will not be reflected in it. See Accessing the Inventory in the README.txt file for more information on the inventory structure and how to access the latest snapshot. Q: What does LastModifiedDate in the inventory CSV represent? A: LastModifiedDate is the object creation date or the last modified date of the JSON metadata object (documented in the README.txt file) for that article version, whichever is the latest. It reflects the last time the JSON metadata object for that version was written to the S3 bucket, which can happen for reasons unrelated to content changes (e.g., metadata enrichment, reprocessing runs, or schema updates). Q: Can the same PMCID appear in both the "open access"[filter] and "author manuscript"[filter] search filters? A: Yes. The most common reason is that an author manuscript has a Creative Commons license — in that case, it qualifies as open access and will be returned by both search filters even if there is only one version of the article in the dataset. A PMCID may also appear in both search filters if it has multiple versions, one of which is an open access published article and another of which is an author manuscript. When building workflows that depend on specific version types, use the JSON metadata for each version to determine its type and license rather than relying solely on search filter results. Search PMC Full-Text Archive Search in PMC Journal List User Guide For Authors PubMed Central (PMC) is a free full-text archive of biomedical and life sciences journal literature managed by the National Library of Medicine (NLM) at the National Institutes of Health (NIH). PMC also serves as the designated repository for papers submitted in accordance with the NIH Public Access Policy and for those that fall under similar policies from other funding agencies . This webpage aims to help authors determine whether their paper is eligible for submission to PMC, how it may be deposited, and by whom. Determining Eligibility Your paper may be included in PMC if You published in a journal that is fully archived in PMC; You made open access arrangements with a PMC selective deposit journal or publisher program; or Your article was supported by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), another PMC designated funder, or a member of the Europe PMC Funders Group; peer reviewed; and accepted for publication in a journal. Determining Submission Method Publisher versions of journal articles are deposited directly by the journal or publisher to PMC; no author action is required to do so. Author Accepted Manuscripts (AAMs) are generally deposited through the NIH Manuscript Submission (NIHMS) system. Note that AAMs supported by members of the Europe PMC Funders Group are submitted through Europe PMC Plus. Author review and approval is required for all AAM submissions. Note that in select cases, an author may need to deposit the AAM to NIHMS to comply with funder requirements. For example, if a journal deposits the final published article with an embargo, an author may need to submit an AAM to be made immediately available upon publication. To determine which way your paper will be submitted, follow the steps below. Step 1: Check the Journal List To find out if the final published article is submitted directly to PMC, see the Journal List . Journals for which complete contents are submitted to PMC are listed as "Agreement to Deposit: All articles". Journals for which only NIH-supported articles are submitted to PMC are listed as "Agreement to Deposit: NIH funded articles". Default embargoes for journals are displayed on the Journal List as well. See the figure below where this information is highlighted. Tips for Funded Authors If a journal is listed as "Agreement to Deposit: NIH funded articles" and your paper was not supported by NIH, proceed to Step 2. If your funder requires immediate availability of your funded paper in PMC and it is published in a journal on the Journal List with a default embargo, you need to either make special arrangements with the journal or publisher to have the final published article deposited without embargo or proceed to Step 3. Note that under the 2024 NIH Public Access Policy , NIH funded articles accepted for publication on or after July 1, 2025, must be made available without embargo upon the Official Date of Publication. Step 2: Review the Selective Deposit Programs Even if a journal does not participate in PMC, the publisher may deposit an article directly to PMC without author involvement if open access arrangements were made and one of these additional submission criteria are met: The article is published in a MEDLINE-indexed journal; or The article acknowledges support of a PMC designated funder or a member of the Europe PMC Funders Group . A list of Selective Deposit Programs can be found on the Selective Deposit Collections page. Always confirm with your publisher directly that they will use this deposit option for your paper if you make such arrangements. Step 3. Deposit the Author Accepted Manuscript If neither of the above deposit options apply, you may deposit your author accepted manuscript to one of two manuscript submission systems to comply with a designated funder policy: NIH Manuscript Submission (NIHMS) System Europe PMC Plus The NIHMS is operated by the National Library of Medicine. The list of funder policies that NIHMS supports is available on the NIHMS Funders page . NIHMS Europe PMC Plus is operated by the European Bioinformatics Institute (EBI). The list of funder policies that EPMC Plus supports is available from the Europe PMC website . Europe PMC Tips for Funded Authors Start your deposit at the time of acceptance for publication. This ensures you have the files readily accessible and allows for manuscript processing times, which may take up to 4 weeks during periods of high volume submissions. If your research was supported by a NIHMS funder and a Europe PMC funder: You only need to deposit the manuscript once. All manuscripts are made discoverable in both PMC and Europe PMC. Submit to the manuscript system that partners with the funder who has stricter embargo and license requirements. Obtaining a PMCID Funders or institutions may request a PMCID as evidence of compliance with any public or open access policies. A PMCID is assigned once a submission has been received by PMC and loaded to the database. A PMCID will be assigned even if an article is under embargo. Tips for Funded Authors Upon deposit to NIHMS or Europe PMC Plus a manuscript identifier will be assigned. NIH-funded researchers can use the NIHMSID as evidence of compliance for up to 3 months after the publication of a paper. After that, a PMCID is required. Not sure if your article has a PMCID? Enter the DOI for your article into the PMC ID Converter . If the article is in PMC, the PMC ID Converter will return the PMCID and other related identifiers.
