The Nemotron RL Litmus-Bench V2.0 dataset and benchmark trains and evaluates LLMs and agentic AI models on molecular properties. A practical recipe post-trains Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for scientific use cases by building a custom reinforcement learning environment from experimental data using NeMo Gym and applying RL with NVIDIA NeMo RL. In a drug-metabolism prediction example, supervised fine-tuning improved accuracy by 12% and RL post-training lifted it a further 17% at a 16,384-token output budget. An optional distillation step uses a stronger teacher model such as Claude Sonnet 5.5 to generate high-quality reasoning traces that warm-start the student model before RL, accelerating convergence. Next Steps Explore the NeMo Gym repository to build a custom RL environment from experimental data. Explore the NeMo RL repository to apply reinforcement learning post-training. Use the recipe as an example to build and evaluate an environment for a specific scientific task. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Agentic AI is reshaping scientific research and innovation. Researchers communicate complex scientific hypotheses in natural language and let autonomous agents independently plan tasks, execute simulations, evaluate results, and self-correct across multiple iterations. Scientific agents are taking on longer, more complex, and increasingly visual workflows. Accuracy and inference efficiency matter at every step. Without verification, errors compound across the workflow, while latency and compute costs multiply with continued operation. NVIDIA Nemotron for Science, a collection of models, datasets, tools, and recipes for accelerating agentic scientific workloads, addresses these hurdles. It includes Nemotron 3.5 Super VL —an open, customizable, multimodal mode l for these specialized workflows—and the NVIDIA Nemotron Litmus-Bench V2.0 , an open source chemistry-reasoning dataset and benchmark that was designed to train and evaluate LLMs and agentic AI models on molecular properties. Out of the box, Nemotron delivers frontier level accuracy for scientific benchmarks (see Figure 1 below), along with the fastest time to solution for scientific coding. Figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL accuracy results across several scientific benchmarks (higher is better) An important benefit of Nemotron models is NVIDIA post-training support. You can customize models for your specific research domain to increase accuracy. This blog provides a practical recipe for post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for scientific use cases. Starting from a raw experimental dataset, you’ll walk through how to build a custom reinforcement learning (RL) environment using NVIDIA NeMo Gym , apply RL, and measure improvement using molecular similarity scoring. NeMo Gym supplies the environment infrastructure, and NVIDIA NeMo RL supplies the post-training framework. This guide uses drug-metabolism prediction as a practical example. Given a parent compound, the starting molecule, and its transforming enzyme, the model predicts the resulting metabolite. The examples below use records from MetxBioDB, which is a comprehensive database of experimentally confirmed biotransformation reactions. The blog first describes direct RL, then an optional distillation step that can be used before RL when a teacher model provides useful examples. Build the reinforcement learning environment from experimental data The starting point is a CSV file of existing experimental records such as sequences, Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) strings, reaction conditions, and any other metadata paired with measured properties or outcomes. In this example, molecular structures are represented as SMILES strings, a text notation for describing a molecule’s atoms and bonds. These input-output pairs are reformatted as question-answer or user/assistant prompt pairs, with the experimental ground truth serving as a verifier to score the model’s responses. This setup constitutes a basic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) environment and requires no human preference labelling: The reward signal comes directly from the data. The fidelity of that reward signal can be tuned to the task. A simple sequence-similarity function works as a lightweight verifier, while more sophisticated tools like cheminformatics libraries, molecular simulators, or even a live autonomous lab can be a tool call and can all be wired in as the environment’s scoring layer. The richer the tool, the more precisely the model is steered toward chemically or biologically meaningful outputs. For the metabolism example, the model receives the parent molecule and enzyme, then submits a predicted metabolite. The verifier compares the predicted and reference molecular fingerprints—numerical representations of structural features—using Tanimoto similarity. Tanimoto similarity is a metric used to measure the overlap between two sets or binary vectors and is calculated by dividing the size of their intersection by the size of their union. For the bit fingerprints used here, the score ranges from 0 to 1; higher scores indicate more similar fingerprints. Figure 2. It combines a pluggable DCIM provider, event-driven rendering, ZTP, DHCP, workflow automation, and configuration storage behind a single Helm deployment. Nautobot is the bundled reference provider and default deployment, not a core-service dependency. NVCM is currently in Developer Preview and is not recommended for production use. Hosted documentation · AI Builders community · Issue tracker · Public release process Overview Service Description ZTP Zero Touch Provisioning, boot scripts, OS image delivery, and provisioning status updates DHCP Kea DHCP configuration generation from selected DCIM-provider data Temporal Long-running network operations and approval workflows Render Template rendering from provider-neutral render data and provider-owned change events Config Store PostgreSQL-backed rendered, intended, and backup configuration storage UI React/Next.js interface for workflows and configuration browsing Nautobot Bundled DCIM provider, custom jobs, and event publication Installer The NVIDIA Config Manager Installer is the supported deployment entry point. It provides an interactive TUI and a headless CLI that both use the same nv-config-manager-install.yaml configuration file. cd installer uv sync uv run nv-config-manager-installer init Common non-interactive commands: cd installer uv run nv-config-manager-installer validate ../deploy/configs/local-superpod.yaml uv run nv-config-manager-installer generate-values ../deploy/configs/local-superpod.yaml --output-dir ../generated uv run nv-config-manager-installer deploy ../deploy/configs/local-superpod.yaml \ --image-source local \ --build-images \ --load-kind \ --kind-cluster nv-config-manager \ --install-envoy-gateway \ --install-cnpg-operator \ --install-cert-manager The installer handles Helm values generation, Kubernetes secrets, optional operator installation, image builds, Kind image loading, content PVC staging, ZTP OS image staging, post-deploy Nautobot jobs, and endpoint reporting. Local Development Setup Install project tools and dependencies before running tests or local deployments. curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh uv sync --dev ./scripts/install-hooks.sh Git Hooks Install the repository hooks after cloning and whenever hook scripts change: ./scripts/install-hooks.sh Installed hooks: pre-commit : checks opted-in OpenPGP, SSH, or X.509/S/MIME signing, formats all staged Python files outside ignored/generated directories with uv run ruff format , re-stages those files, and checks SPDX license headers for supported source files ( .py , .ts , .tsx , .js , .jsx , .mjs , .cjs , and .go ) under src/ , ui/src/ , ui/tests/ , components/ , db/migrations/ , scripts/ , development/ , installer/src/ , installer/tests/ , and installer/scripts/ . commit-msg : rejects commits that do not include a valid DCO Signed-off-by: Name <email> trailer. Use git commit -s or git commit --amend -s to add the trailer automatically. The hook installer reports signing readiness only when repository-local signing settings are present. Trustees need GitHub-verified commits for automatic sync and should follow the internal signing setup guidance. Other contributors and draft pull requests instead need an authorized maintainer to approve the exact commit with /ok to test <sha> ; they are not prompted to configure a signing key. See Cryptographically Signing Commits for the trustee and non-trustee workflows. The local signing check is advisory. GitHub and copy-pr-bot make the authoritative decision about signature verification and protected CI branch creation. Local hooks can be skipped with git commit --no-verify ; maintainers must still ensure every commit satisfies the DCO before accepting a contribution. For UI work: cd ui npm install Validation commands: make test uv run ruff check src/ uv run mypy src/ uv run ruff format src/ Kubernetes Deployment Prerequisites: Docker or a compatible container runtime Kind for local clusters, or a reachable Kubernetes cluster Helm 3.x kubectl configured for the target cluster Python 3.11 or newer, managed through uv Node.js 23 or newer for UI development Resource Profiles Res

search_index.title: Amid Ecosystem Adoption, NVIDIA Opens Vera Rubin Architecture to Help Scale AI Factories Worldwide | NVIDIA Blog
search_index.description: Cisco, Google, Meta, Microsoft and Visionbay are joining many making advances with Vera Rubin.
search_index.content: Amid Ecosystem Adoption, NVIDIA Opens Vera Rubin Architecture to Help Scale AI Factories Worldwide | NVIDIA Blog Skip to content As AI factories grow from megawatts to gigawatts, building them takes more than advanced computing. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably. At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, NVIDIA announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at creating a common foundation for next-generation AI infrastructure. NVIDIA contributed key NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack and compute tray designs to OCP through the open NVIDIA MGX architecture, giving system builders a common foundation for developing next-generation AI factory infrastructure. Together, these efforts span the AI factory itself, the utility grid that powers it and the rack-scale architecture at the heart of modern accelerated computing. NVIDIA and Partners Announce Open Architecture Advances At the OCP event, NVIDIA and partners made a handful of announcements: NVIDIA and hyperscalers published open standards for next-generation AI factories, including AI factory design standards and grid resilience. NVIDIA launched new open source software components for NVIDIA DSX AI Factory. Meta and NVIDIA advanced open AI networking with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet SuperNIC and Spectrum-6 innovations. Visionbay introduced an 800V DC AI factory design for the Vera Rubin era. NVIDIA and Cisco announced the Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) standard, the industry’s first module ​for 400Gb/s-based networking fabrics. NVIDIA and Google announced Falcon Transport support on future NVIDIA ConnectX-10 SuperNICs and BlueField DPUs. Before a packed audience, Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, discussed how open infrastructure is becoming a critical ingredient for scaling AI factories worldwide. The news at OCP spotlights how NVIDIA’s extreme codesign combined with open standards is accelerating deployment, improving power efficiency and driving tokens-per-watt performance. Vera Rubin AI Factories Advance With MGX Rack Contributions at OCP 🔗 NVIDIA joined industry leaders in contributing to the third-generation MGX AI data center reference design through OCP’s Open DC Initiative. Combined with open liquid-cooling technologies such as MQD and MQDB, the effort helps turn proven AI factory designs into industry standards that others can adopt, manufacture and scale. For NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories, the updated MGX 1.2 specification extends the open architecture for AI factories with rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar designed for higher-power AI systems. It also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs. MGX 1.2 further expands modularity with configurable I/O bays, fanless liquid-cooled compute trays, standardized power and cooling interfaces, and a common infrastructure that helps ecosystem partners build interoperable accelerated computing platforms. It improves assembly, test and service times to streamline manufacturing and field service to enable faster and more efficient infrastructure buildout. The architecture supports rack deployments up to 250kW while simplifying serviceability, deployment and infrastructure reuse. The Vera CPU rack design specification extends the NVIDIA MGX open architecture beyond accelerated computing, providing a purpose-built platform for the growing agentic AI era. While Vera Rubin NVL72 serves as the foundation for large-scale training and inference, the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack is designed to support tool calling, orchestration and sandboxed execution, helping AI agents interact with applications, data and services in real time. Built on the third-generation NVIDIA MGX rack architecture, the Vera CPU rack shares the same rack-scale design principles that unite compute, networking, power and cooling into a common modular platform. This approach enables partners to deploy specialized infrastructure while benefiting from a shared ecosystem, simplified integration and a consistent foundation for next-generation AI factories. At the center of this unified system is DSX OS, the open operating layer that turns the DSX architecture into coordinated, repeatable operations at scale. At OCP, NVIDIA expanded DSX OS with open source components for configuring networks, validating clusters, managing racks and provisioning bare metal: NVIDIA Config Manager : Automates switch configurations at scale, allowing customers to deploy, validate and maintain consistent AI factory network fabrics with minimal to zero manual intervention. NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine : Helps eliminate costly job crashes by stress-testing GPU clusters with real workload simulations to guarantee hardware health before training begins. NVIDIA Rack Management Service : Offers a rack hardware abstraction and operations solutions that treats racks as first-class units for improved AI factory scale firmware management. Cluster API Provider for NVIDIA Infrastructure Controller : Accelerates bare-metal deployment and tenant onboarding, turning raw AI hardware into production-ready clusters in hours instead of days. Developed from NVIDIA’s experience running NVIDIA DGX Cloud, these open source components enable cloud providers and software partners to integrate AI factory capabilities directly into their multi-tenant platforms. search_index.title: How Companies Are Using NVIDIA DSX to Break the Power Bottleneck | NVIDIA Blog
search_index.description: Companies around the world are using the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform to plan, simulate and run AI factories as one system and unlock infrastructure development.
search_index.content: How Companies Are Using NVIDIA DSX to Break the Power Bottleneck | NVIDIA Blog Skip to content Companies around the world are building on the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform to plan, simulate and run the grid and the AI factory as one system, from the substation to the rack. Their adoption of the platform responds to an acute problem. Power is now the biggest bottleneck in infrastructure. More than $300 billion in equipment is backlogged, and over 200 gigawatts of projects are waiting in U.S. interconnection queues. One root cause of the bottleneck is siloed systems. The grid, the facility and the compute inside have long been designed independently from one another, creating the conditions for delays, risk and stranded capacity. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements To help address this, NVIDIA DSX brings these systems together: NVIDIA DSX Sim and SimReady assets from leading energy manufacturers let engineers simulate the grid, substation and AI factory together, validating generators, switchgear, power systems and cooling before breaking ground. NVIDIA DSX Flex syncs AI factory demand with grid conditions and onsite generation, turning AI factories from static loads into flexible grid assets. NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS and DSX Exchange squeeze more compute from every watt and securely share signals across compute, networking, energy, cooling and operations. GE Vernova is deploying its grid-to-facility and rack power expertise to complement NVIDIA DSX systems, enabling customers to transform power constraints into competitive advantages while maximizing compute and token output, sustainability and grid reliability. Hitachi Energy ’s battery energy storage system has qualified as NVIDIA DSX Ready , helping customers identify power infrastructure that meets applicable NVIDIA DSX reference architecture design requirements for resilient, reliable and scalable AI factories. Schneider Electric , together with AVEVA and ETAP, is advancing NVIDIA DSX with validated NVIDIA Vera Rubin power and cooling reference architectures and an NVIDIA Omniverse -powered AI factory digital twin. Combining AVEVA ’s engineering software expertise with NVIDIA SimReady assets, OpenUSD and Omniverse enables connecting simulations, real-time operational data and AI-driven optimization across AVEVA, Schneider Electric and third-party solutions. Together, these capabilities help organizations design, simulate, operate and optimize data centers across their lifecycle, improving energy efficiency and workload performance while accelerating time to token. Siemens Energy is expanding its collaboration with NVIDIA by developing a reference design for resilient, scalable and grid-aware power infrastructure across power generation, transmission and distribution. This design is aligned with the requirements of the NVIDIA DSX Vera Rubin AI factory design. The company is also exploring usingNVIDIA technologies such as RAPIDS, Metropolis and Isaac Sim for its Noedra digital twin platform, evaluating how the technologies could enhance grid infrastructure monitoring, identify emerging risks and support unplanned outage prevention. Phaidra integrated DSX Flex, DSX Max-Q and DSX Exchange into its self-learning agents, optimizing cooling and power allocation to maximize tokens per watt, improve grid flexibility and deliver about 10% more compute within the same power envelope. Emerald AI integrated its Conductor platform into DSX Flex to help utilities tap underused grid capacity, an approach modeled to unlock up to 100 gigawatts on the existing U.S. grid. search_index.description: NVIDIA today announced the NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory reference design, a guide for building codesigned AI infrastructure, and general availability of the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint, fully compatible with NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX, to enable physically accurate AI factory digital twins for lar
search_index.content: NVIDIA Releases Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory Reference Design and Omniverse DSX Digital Twin Blueprint With Broad Industry Support | NVIDIA Newsroom NVIDIA Releases Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory Reference Design and Omniverse DSX Digital Twin Blueprint With Broad Industry Support March 16, 2026 News Summary: The new NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory reference design provides a guide for building codesigned AI infrastructure that delivers maximum token per watt and accelerated time to first production. The NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint, now generally available with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI Factory reference design, powers digital twins for large-scale AI factory design and simulation. Industry leaders Cadence, Dassault Systèmes, Eaton, Jacobs, NScale, Phaidra, Procore Technologies, PTC, Schneider Electric, Siemens, Switch, Trane Technologies and Vertiv are contributing to the DSX architecture and blueprint by integrating platforms, providing SimReady assets and connecting software to help design, build and optimize AI factories. Energy leaders Emerald AI, GE Vernova, Hitachi and Siemens Energy are using the NVIDIA DSX reference architecture to unlock grid capacity, delivering the power needed to build and connect new AI factories. GTC— NVIDIA today announced the NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory reference design, a guide for building codesigned AI infrastructure, and general availability of the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint , fully compatible with NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX, to enable physically accurate AI factory digital twins for large-scale design, buildout and operations. Industry leaders Cadence , Dassault Systèmes , Eaton , Jacobs , Nscale , Phaidra , Procore , PTC , Schneider Electric , Siemens , Switch , Trane Technologies and Vertiv are contributing to the reference design and blueprint to help plan, build and operate these massive AI factory buildouts. “In the age of AI, intelligence tokens are the new currency, and AI factories are the infrastructure that generates them,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “With the NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory reference design and Omniverse DSX Blueprint, we are providing the foundation to build the world’s most productive AI factories, accelerating time to first revenue and maximizing scale and energy efficiency.” Building AI Factories That Maximize Every Watt Building large-scale AI factories to meet the rising demand for training and inference is complex, requiring precise coordination across infrastructure, power, cooling, networking, software and compute. The NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory reference design outlines how to design, build and operate the entire AI factory infrastructure stack, spanning compute, NVIDIA Spectrum-X™ Ethernet networking and storage, for repeatable, scalable and optimal cluster performance. Documentation within the reference design also equips industry partners with best practices to design, build and operate power, cooling and control systems, enabling seamless hardware-software integration and scalable deployment. The Vera Rubin DSX software stack is open, modular and composable, connecting cluster hardware with power and cooling to maximize AI tokens per watt of available energy. Its flexible design lets AI factory builders and data center providers deploy as many components as they need. Rubin DSX offers a collection of software libraries for partners to build on: DSX Max-Q helps AI factories and ecosystem partners maximize computing output and token performance per watt on NVIDIA systems within a fixed power budget. DSX Flex connects AI factories to power-grid services, enabling them to dynamically adjust power use and orchestrate demand with hybrid onsite generation to save energy and maintain grid stability. DSX Exchange enables scalable and secure integration of compute, network, energy, power and cooling plant signals between IT, operational technology and operations agents. DSX Sim models validate AI factories as high-fidelity digital twins, using the NVIDIA DSX Air platform to model GPUs, networking and partner infrastructure, and DSX SimReady connects detailed 3D geometry, logistics and system behavior — accelerating time to first revenue and ensuring day-one performance. Accelerating AI Factory Design and Simulation Even with a detailed architecture, designing, building and operating large-scale AI factories can be difficult. Traditional design methods are limited in their ability to model entire systems, be flexible and efficient with power use, and validate designs before construction begins. The NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint provides an open, comprehensive framework for designing and operating large-scale AI factories. Now generally available on build.nvidia.com and fully compatible with the Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory reference design, Omniverse DSX allows developers to build physically accurate digital twins of their AI factories, simulate operations in real time and optimize performance before construction or deployment begins. Omniverse DSX unifies power, cooling, networking and operations in one environment to accelerate time to revenue and AI efficiency. Using NVIDIA Omniverse ™ libraries, companies can simulate layouts, power topologies, thermal behavior and operational policies — and evaluate hardware or workload changes without disrupting production. Industry Leaders Embrace New Reference Design and Blueprint Reliable, scalable power and cooling are the backbone of every AI factory, enabling intelligent systems to adapt in real time to changing compute demands while maximizing efficiency and uptime. A broad ecosystem of partners, from energy to software leaders, are embracing DSX to transform the full AI factory lifecycle into a seamlessly optimized product-level system, codesigned for resilience, precision and efficiency. search_index.title: NVIDIA Announces Collaboration With IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory to Launch Quantum-Classical Codesign Platform, Plus Error-Correction Breakthrough to Advance Practical Quantum Computi
search_index.description: NVIDIA today announced plans for new collaborations with IBM and the U.S. Department of Energy’s Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory that will span research into next-generation modular architectures for quantum computers, scientific applications and supercomputing integration.
search_index.content: NVIDIA Announces Collaboration With IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory to Launch Quantum-Classical Codesign Platform, Plus Error-Correction Breakthrough to Advance Practical Quantum Computing | NVIDIA Newsroom NVIDIA Announces Collaboration With IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory to Launch Quantum-Classical Codesign Platform, Plus Error-Correction Breakthrough to Advance Practical Quantum Computing IBM and NVIDIA Work With Fermilab in Developing Modular Architectures for Scalable Quantum Computers — Separately, Breakthrough NVIDIA CUDA-Q Algorithm Delivers up to 13,000x Faster Decoding for Error-Correction Research November 16, 2026 News Summary: NVIDIA and IBM announce a growing quantum supercomputing collaboration combining NVIDIA accelerated computing and software with IBM quantum computers to advance quantum error-correction research, scientific applications and integration into supercomputing workflows. NVIDIA DGX B200 systems will connect with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, the most powerful processor IBM has yet built. A quantum computing codesign platform with Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, alongside IBM and NVIDIA, will support quantum error-correction and applications research for future systems. NVIDIA releases TCBP-JOBS, a new decoding algorithm part of the CUDA-Q platform, that delivers up to a 13,000x speedup for quantum error-correction research, accelerating fault-tolerant quantum computation. NVIDIA is expanding Slurm to simplify scheduling quantum processors within supercomputing workflows, with IBM contributing integration through its Quantum Resource Management Interface. NVIDIA today announced plans for new collaborations with IBM and the U.S. Department of Energy’s Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory that will span research into next-generation modular architectures for quantum computers, scientific applications and supercomputing integration. These efforts, including a new modular quantum computing codesign platform with IBM and Fermilab, combine NVIDIA accelerated computing and software with IBM quantum computers to help researchers scale quantum computers and explore their scientific capabilities. Separately, NVIDIA also announced a new quantum algorithm that delivers up to 13,000x faster decoding compared with existing leading algorithms — cutting the computation time for researching new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to just 45 minutes. The collaboration with IBM also brings together new Slurm capabilities integrations to simplify how quantum computers can be added into supercomputing workflows. Modular Quantum Computing Codesign Platform IBM and NVIDIA are colocating NVIDIA DGX™ B200 systems with state-of-the-art IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, the fastest quantum processor IBM has ever delivered. This integrated system is supporting a jointly developed IBM, Fermilab and NVIDIA modular quantum codesign platform. The codesign platform will allow researchers to develop and evaluate error-correction codes, decoding algorithms and quantum-classical applications driving scientific discoveries in high-energy and nuclear physics (HENP), as well as how classical systems can scale alongside multiple linked quantum processors within modular architectures. Fermilab’s expertise will allow work at the platform to focus on quantum error correction and HENP applications — helping define requirements for future fault-tolerant quantum computers and the science that can be achieved with them. “Making quantum computers useful for science requires advances in error correction, applications and the systems that bring quantum processors and accelerated computing together,” said Krysta Svore, vice president of applied research for quantum computing at NVIDIA. “NVIDIA’s research software and our collaboration with IBM give scientists more powerful tools to investigate quantum designs and develop applications across these systems.” “Some of the most fundamental problems in science remain out of reach without access to quantum computing. Scaling quantum and classical together will open new frontiers in high-energy and nuclear physics and beyond,” said Jerry Chow, IBM Fellow and chief technology officer of quantum-centric computing. “With Fermilab and NVIDIA, we plan to explore how these real-world problems can help us shape the modular, interconnected architectures that will define the next generation of quantum computers and accelerated classical computing.” “The future of quantum computing depends on more than advances in quantum hardware alone,” said Anna Grassellino, Fermilab chief technology officer and director of the SQMS Center. “Accelerated computing and superintelligence will play an important role in how we design algorithms, study errors and coordinate increasingly complex quantum systems. This proposed platform would combine NVIDIA’s computing capabilities with IBM’s quantum technologies and Fermilab’s scientific expertise, and would enable researchers to explore new approaches to codesigning quantum computers that meet the needs of challenging HENP science problems.” Advancing Quantum Error-Correction Research Errors inherent to quantum processors limit the complexity and duration of the computations they can perform. Quantum error correction protects quantum information by encoding it across multiple physical qubits. A classical algorithm called a decoder interprets measurement data to identify likely errors so they can be corrected. Available through the NVIDIA CUDA-Q™ QEC 0.9.0 library today, NVIDIA’s new TCBP-JOBS decoding algorithm accelerates the computationally intensive parts of quantum error-correction research by up to 13,000x while delivering high accuracy. U.S. dollars for WTI oil and 115.54 U.S. dollars for the OPEC basket. Oil prices rose slightly that week. Europe's Brent crude oil, the U.S. WTI crude oil, and OPEC's basket are three of the most important benchmarks used by traders as references for global oil and gasoline prices . Lowest ever oil prices during coronavirus pandemic In 2020, the coronavirus pandemic resulted in crude oil prices hitting a major slump as oil demand drastically declined following lockdowns and travel restrictions. Initial outlooks and uncertainty surrounding the course of the pandemic brought about a disagreement between two of the largest oil producers, Russia and Saudi Arabia, in early March. Bilateral talks between global oil producers ended in agreement on April 13th, with promises to cut petroleum output and hopes rising that these might help stabilize the oil price in the coming weeks. However, with storage facilities and oil tankers quickly filling up, fears grew over where to store excess oil, leading to benchmark prices seeing record negative prices between April 20 and April 22, 2020. How crude oil prices are determined As with most commodities, crude oil prices are impacted by supply and demand, as well as inventories and market sentiment. However, as oil is most often traded in future contracts (where a contract is agreed upon while product delivery will follow in the next two to three months), market speculation is one of the principal determinants for oil prices. Traders make conclusions on how production output and consumer demand will likely develop over the coming months, leaving room for uncertainty. Spot prices differ from futures in so far as they reflect the current market price of a commodity. When looking solely at laptop CPUs, Intel is the clear winner, accounting for over 70 percent of laptop CPU test benchmark results in the first quarter of 2026. Traditional x86 processors The x86 is a family of instruction set architectures (ISA) for computer processors, otherwise known as central processing units (CPUs), which were initially developed by Intel . They refer to the way a CPU handles information, with x86 architecture of variable instruction lengths, and primarily of a complex instruction set computer (CISC) design. Although additions and developments to the x86 processor have taken place, backward compatibility has remained a key feature of the architecture; the newer x86 processors can run all the programs that older processors could run. Apple Mac processors The x86 processor is the predominant hardware platform for laptops, desktops, and servers globally . Both Windows and Mac laptops have used x86 chips; previously, Apple’s line of Mac products used PowerPC microprocessors, with the transition to Intel x86 architecture first acknowledged in 2005. The first generation of Intel-based Mac computers were released in January 2006, a partnership that continued through until 2020, where Apple announced the switch of the Mac line from Intel CPUs to Arm-based processors. The decision was made in order to standardize on one CPU architecture for all iPhone, iPad, and Mac products. How do music artists get so many streams on Spotify? Firstly, Spotify is one of the most successful and popular music streaming services in the United States , and as of the first half of 2018 had the biggest share of music streaming subscribers in the world . With Spotify’s vast audience, featuring on the platform is a good start for emerging and popular artists hoping to make an impact. Secondly, there is no exact science to ‘going viral’.
